items.articleBody:
Morgen erscheint GTA VI, eines der größten Spiele aller Zeiten. Doch die Menschen, die es gebaut haben, kämpfen vor Gericht und im Unternehmen für ihre Rechte. Der Forscher Jonas Ferdinand erklärt, warum das mehr ist als ein Unternehmensstreit.

Für die gewerkschaftliche Organisierung braucht es keine Waffen, aber Mut und einen langen Atem. – Alle Rechte vorbehalten: Rockstar Games

Vier freie Tage zum Zocken, wenn sie sich für zwei Jahre bei der US-Armee weiterverpflichten: Mit diesem Angebot hat eine [US-Infanteriedivision in Fort Stewart](https://www.tagesspiegel.de/gesellschaft/medien/populares-videospiel-angebot-an-us-soldaten-langerer-dienst-fur-tage-mit-gta-vi-15962901.html) um Soldat:innen geworben. Es ist nur eines von vielen Zeichen für den gigantischen Hype um ein Computerspiel, auf das Fans seit Jahren sehnsüchtig warten.

Morgen, mehr als 13 Jahre nach [GTA V](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Theft_Auto_V), erscheint Grand Theft Auto VI. Doch während sich Millionen Menschen aufs Zocken freuen, kämpfen diejenigen, die das Spiel entwickelt haben, immer noch um ihre Rechte.

Im Herbst 2025 [hat der GTA-Entwickler](https://www.theguardian.com/games/2025/nov/07/uk-union-accuses-gta-maker-rockstar-games-of-firing-employees-attempting-to-organise) Rockstar Games 31 Beschäftigte in Großbritannien entlassen, die sich gewerkschaftlich organisiert hatten. Als den „skrupellosesten Fall von Union Busting in der Geschichte der Games-Branche“, hat das die britische Gewerkschaft [Independent Workers of Great Britain (IWGB) bezeichnet.](https://www.iwgb.org.uk/staff-at-rockstar-fired-en-masse)

Rockstar weist den Vorwurf zurück. Die Betroffenen hätten vertrauliche Informationen in einem Discord-Kanal geteilt, so das Unternehmen [gegenüber Bloomberg](https://www.theregister.com/software/2025/11/06/rockstar-faces-union-protest-in-london-over-leak-sackings/809098). Auf eine Presseanfrage von netzpolitik.org zum Thema hat Rockstar nicht geantwortet.

Viele der Entlassenen haben gegen ihre Kündigungen geklagt. Zeitgleich zum Release von GTA stimmen die Beschäftigten jetzt an den britischen Rockstar-Standorten darüber ab, ob Rockstar die Gewerkschaft IWGB formell anerkennen soll.

Für Jonas Ferdinand, der [beim Weizenbaum-Institut unter anderem zu Arbeit forscht](https://www.weizenbaum-institut.de/portrait/p/jonas-ferdinand/#page=1&tags=science_publications&sort=date), ist der Konflikt weit mehr als eine Firmenangelegenheit. Gemeinsam mit Daniel Jordan von der University of Glasgow hat er eine [Untersuchung zur Mitbestimmung in der Games-Branche](https://wzb.eu/de/artikel/junge-branche-alte-spiele) veröffentlicht.

„Man muss sich den Mut anschauen, den diese Mitarbeiter:innen gezeigt haben, sich dort zu organisieren, den Kampf weiterzuführen und in den Gerichtsprozess zu gehen“, sagt Ferdinand gegenüber netzpolitik.org. Rockstar gehöre zu den bekanntesten und erfolgreichsten Studios der Welt. Die gewerkschaftliche Organisierung bei Rockstar könne einen „Leuchtturmeffekt“ für die ganze Branche haben, so der Games-Experte weiter.

## Crunch, Druck & Unsicherheit

Die Probleme bei Rockstar seien „sehr typisch für die Industrie“, so Ferdinand. Besonders bekannt ist der sogenannte Crunch: Beschäftigte arbeiten in der Schlussphase einer Produktion häufig über Wochen hinweg deutlich länger, um den Veröffentlichungstermin für ein Spiel zu halten. Die Überstunden werden laut Ferdinand häufig weder ausreichend begrenzt noch finanziell kompensiert. Die Folgen reichten bis zu Burnouts und langfristigen gesundheitlichen Schäden. Crunch sei „leider noch gängige Praxis“.

Hinzu kommen intransparente Gehälter, unklare Karrierewege und eine teils toxische Arbeitskultur. Besonders Frauen und Beschäftigte, die nicht dem lange vorherrschenden Bild des jungen, weißen, heterosexuellen Mannes entsprechen, sind davon betroffen, so Ferdinand.

Zugleich verschärfen Entlassungswellen und Studioschließungen die Unsicherheit. Gewerkschaften und Betriebsräte könnten die Beschäftigten im Kampf dagegen unterstützen. Der Organisierungsgrad sei in der Branche jedoch laut Ferdinand noch gering. Viele Angestellte wüssten gar nicht um ihre Rechte.

## „Ein Unternehmen ist keine Familie“

Warum organisieren sich trotz dieser Probleme so wenige Beschäftigte? Ein Grund ist die Angst vor beruflichen Nachteilen. Selbst in Deutschland, wo Beschäftigte vergleichsweise starke Mitbestimmungsrechte haben, ist es nicht selbstverständlich, diese einzufordern, so Ferdinand.

Wer in Deutschland einen Betriebsrat gründe oder sich gewerkschaftlich organisiere, riskiere, bei der nächsten Jobsuche Schwierigkeiten zu bekommen. Und weil immer mehr Menschen auf einen Job in der Branche warteten, stehe der Ersatz schon bereit. „Das macht das Risiko natürlich größer“, betont Ferdinand.

Besonders hart treffe es internationale Beschäftigte, deren Visum am Job hängt und damit auch ihr gesamtes Leben und ihre Familie. „Wenn der Arbeitsplatz so schon unter Druck ist, kann man sich ja vorstellen, wie schwierig es ist, sich unter diesen Bedingungen einzusetzen“, sagt Ferdinand.

Viele seien zudem von der Leidenschaft für Spiele und der kreativen Arbeit angetrieben. Diese persönliche Begeisterung lasse die Entwickler:innen schlechte Arbeitsbedingungen eher hinnehmen, vor allem in Studios mit Start-up-Mentalität und einer familiären Betriebskultur. Ferdinand hält diese Vorstellung für problematisch: „Ein Unternehmen ist keine Familie.“ Überstunden müssten kompensiert werden und Transparenz müsse gewährleistet sein.

## Vom Bier in der Kneipe zum Betriebsrat

In den vergangenen Jahren habe sich jedoch etwas verändert. Gewerkschaften hätten die Bedeutung der Games-Branche erkannt und unterstützten dabei, Kontakte zu knüpfen. „Das gab es lange nicht“, sagt Ferdinand. Früher hätten viele gedacht: „Es gibt ja gar keine Gewerkschaft für mich. Ich kann meine Arbeitsbedingungen ja gar nicht mehr verändern.“

In Deutschland hat ver.di den [Game Dev Roundtable](https://www.verdi.de/ikt-nrw/themen-und-kampagnen/game-devs) als Anlaufstelle für Beschäftigte und Betriebsratsgründungen ins Leben gerufen. Mit Erfolg: Aus dem Netzwerk sind laut Ferdinand in den letzten Jahren fast 20 Betriebsräte entstanden.

Oft beginnt Organisierung ganz unspektakulär, erzählt Ferdinand: „Die Leute miteinander zu vernetzen, sich in der Kneipe auf ein Bier zu treffen“ seien wichtige erste Schritte. Es gehe darum, Vertrauen aufzubauen, bevor Konflikte eskalieren. Auch international tauschen Gewerkschaften Erfahrungen und Materialien.

## Mehr Mitbestimmung gegen Überstunden und Überwachung

Betriebsräte können in Deutschland bei Arbeitszeiten und Überstunden mitreden, Regelungen zum Ausgleich von Crunch verhandeln und bei Entlassungen auf Interessenausgleich und Sozialpläne hinwirken.

items.articleBody:
No one is well served by listening to pedants, but I think I’ve found an exception.

This past weekend, I was a reader at *The Power Broker* Marathon, where 400+ volunteers took turns reading the entirety of Robert Caro’s magisterial book, in ten minute chunks, over the course of 66 hours. The event’s organizers found their readers through an open call. A startling number of my friends and family forwarded the sign up form to me. It asked, among other things, when you would be available to read. I selected “Afternoon,” “Evening,” and after a pause, “Morning” too. I’m an early riser with a young son, after all, so I didn’t foresee any issues.

A few week’s later I got my assigned time: 3:10 AM on Sunday. Technically, a morning slot. But I’m more of a fan of Robert Caro than I am of sleeping in. I confirmed.

I’m a devoted reader of Caro, and I’ve taken up the Bob beat on Lit Hub too, where I’ve covered fellow [Caro-heads](https://lithub.com/caro-head-matthew-rhys-wants-to-make-a-power-broker-show-with-netflix/), his [posts on Instagram](https://lithub.com/attention-lbj-nerds-robert-caro-is-posting-book-updates-on-instagram/), and [the 50th anniversary of The Power Broker](https://lithub.com/50-facts-about-the-power-broker-to-celebrate-its-50th-anniversary/), Caro’s 1162 page book about Robert Moses and his transformative tenure as New York City Parks Commissioner, during which he built miles and acres of highways, roads, bridges, and parks, at the expense of low-income families, farmers, and other less powerful New Yorkers. It’s a great book.

So much to say, I had no trouble popping up with my 1:15 AM alarm and heading out into the cold to read. I traveled northwest across Brooklyn towards the harbor, where the marathon was 50-hours or more old, having stretched from Thursday, through Friday, Saturday, and now into Sunday. I guessed that the story was probably well into the mayoralty of Robert Wagner at that point. I walked by a few giggly couples, walking in the other direction and on a different timeline, enjoying the end of their late Saturday, and soon found myself at Judgy Baby.

Judgy Baby is an industrial warehouse space in the shadow of Moses’s Gowanus Parkway; the event was organized by Brad Vogel, their director of special projects. Vogel told [The New York Groove](https://nygroove.nyc/power-broker-marathon/) that the idea for the marathon came out of a *Power Broker* reading group he ran last year.

“Instead of people saying ‘no that’s ridiculous,’” he said, “people were actually excited.”

I’d seen the set-up inside on social media, later covered glossily in places like *[The Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/nyregion/power-broker-marathon-reading-robert-moses-caro.html?unlocked_article_code=1.Q1E.VR6m.qJA-ZjHN3cO1)*: a banner, a microphone, and a podium with a copy of the book. In pictures of the marathon’s opening, the stage was filled with luminaries like Caro’s editor, the voice of the NY subway system, and a number of current government officials. *Power Broker* fans are everywhere, like some kind of nerd Illuminati.

None of those big names were in attendance when I arrived at 2:00 AM, but I was happy to see a small and dedicated crew of volunteers, readers, and fans. The big warehouse was much livelier than I’d anticipated; a few people were curled up napping, but the majority were awake: hanging out, chatting, grabbing a quick meal. At least one person was engrossed in a novel. There was coffee, and wine, and a pile of commemorative t-shirts. I took a cup of coffee and a small.

A volunteer checked me in and oriented me. When it was my time, a volunteer would point out where the last reader had left off, and then step back on stage when my ten minutes were up, when I would need to find a natural place to stop. He stressed that this might not be the end of a full sentence, so I might need to find a comma to pause on. Caro is long winded, I was warned, but little did this volunteer know that I was *hoping* for one of Caro’s famous lists to be in my section (though the most famous one, [inspired by Homer,](https://www.theparisreview.org/interviews/6442/the-art-of-biography-no-5-robert-caro#:~:text=how%20do%20you%20make%20people%20grasp%20the%20immensity%20of%20this%3F%20And%20I%20remembered%20reading%20the%20Iliad%20in%20college%2E%20The%20Iliad%20did%20it%20with%20lists%2C%20you%20know%3F) had already long passed.)

I was also asked to read slowly, if I could. The readers before me had been over-eager, and the marathon was ahead of schedule. Caro really does get people excited.

I still had about an hour until my slot, so I found a seat in a back pew (appropriately devotional seating) and listened. In the book, the Tavern on the Green controversy was just coming to a head, one of the rare moments when Moses was personally exposed to public scrutiny. One by one, each reader was replaced by a guiding volunteer, with hearty applause at each transition. Unlike a typical reading, there was no introduction of each new reader (though all our names were in a program, in a tiny font). We were each anonymous, a succession of Vestal priestesses keeping the flame of this project warm.

One reader took the slowdown command very literally, and read his section with long and deliberate pauses between each word. There was some delirious laughter at the careful pacing, and he ended with a round of appreciative cheers and applause.

At 2:50 AM, I was shown to a chair next to the stage. To my right was the on-deck reader, with her own copy of the book to follow along. When she was brought on stage, I took her seat and her warm-up *Power Broker*. I forgot how small the typeface was in this book, and immediately started feeling like a panicked sixth grader again, skimming ahead and trying to count paragraphs. We were in chapter 43, “Late Arrival”, with the press finally starting to get wise to Moses and his vast, unelected power. Over 1,000 pages in, Moses was nearing the end of his public life.

And then I was up and [on stage](https://www.youtube.com/live/bZkbDbru2uE?si=bg-c9n4MkH4FVHvb&t=11394), following the volunteer’s finger. “Robert Moses still ran the show,” my section began. I stumbled once or twice—“daises” briefly looked like “daisies,” and I read “Rockefeller 3d” as “three d” until I corrected to “the third.” But I was delighted to find a list in my three pages, a comma-laced sentence detailing all the elements that were a part of Moses’s plan for Lincoln Center.

When my time was up, I rejoined the crowd for a few more pages, and then tiptoed into the green room to gather my things. I talked with a few of the volunteer organizers, and compared notes on how the reading went, when we had first finished the book, and which of Moses’s highways confounded us the most in our daily lives. The bleary but bright-eyed energy reminded me of other big efforts I’d been a part of, like the City Marathon or the WGA Writers Strike. Everyone was stretched, but proud. We were doing something, together, and no one would risk letting the rest down. No wonder we were speeding through the book ahead of schedule.

I took a longer walk home, since my train was skipping stops, and passed under the Gowanus Expressway, feeling the crumbling yet still powerful hand of Moses’s ghost on my shoulder.

The feeling of history’s living nearness is why this book is catnip for New Yorkers. It’s a way for us to navel gaze, to talk about how much we love our big, beautiful, messy town, and to gush about how exceptional it is, that even its flaws are so grand to be worth a thousand pages of beautiful prose. But it’s also a way into our other favorite topic of conversation: which trains are delayed, why, and how it’s ruining our day. As one volunteer put it, reading *The Power Broker* in New York feels like running into an ex—every corner you turn, there Moses is again, standing in your way.

It was nice to be home at 4:30 AM, and nice to know that the Marathon was still marching along. The next day—or rather, later the same morning—I pulled up the livestream on my phone to catch the last sections of the book.

Clocking in to read the last page was [Robert A. Caro himself](https://www.youtube.com/live/zjjQY79wuNM?si=YG28RnZrf6t1b4O0&t=17647), there on pre-recorded video, the final volunteer reader. Watching the livestream on my phone, I misheard the penultimate line, swapping “he” for “we”: “Couldn’t people see what we had done?”

I teared up a little—from sleep deprivation as much as anything else—to hear it in Caro’s thick, New York accent.

items.subtitle: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere.

items.articleBody:
Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company [billions of dollars](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/28/google-alphabet-q3-earnings-report) in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an [AI-powered humanoid robot](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/06/1148090/i-watched-a-humanoid-robot-clean-my-apartment-it-felt-like-a-taste-of-the-future/) up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an [AI-assisted cyberattack](https://www.wired.com/story/kernel-panic-refrigeration-hacks-internet-of-things/).

You go to the movies and see [Sam Altman](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/06/artificial-sam-altman-ai-movie-review) being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a [Grok-fied version of The Odyssey](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/27/elon-musk-ai-odyssey-movie-grok-christopher-nolan). You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

items.articleBody:
Fox News took a liking to the WNBA this past season, but not so much for the basketball and more so for the rage bait. Melanie Walsh, with Jan Diehm, for the Pudding, [analyzed WNBA coverage through chryon data](https://pudding.cool/2026/11/wnba-politics/).

> Fox News’ vocabulary barely touches on-court play. Its coverage is driven by social media reactions and political flashpoints, leaning heavily into conservative buzzwords like “white privilege,” “national anthem,” and “biological men.”
> At the center of this framing sits “Fever star” Clark, whom Fox News repeatedly tethers to its conservative agenda.

Walsh provides an analysis from all angles. The comparison between Fox News coverage against how other networks cover the WNBA shows the baiting most clearly. Whereas the other networks focus more on points and rebounds, Fox News focuses on social media and race.

items.articleBody:
**Mit der Apple Watch Series 12 und der Ultra 4 will Cupertino die Uhr zum digitalen Gedächtnis machen. Ein erster ausführlicher Alltagstest dämpft die Erwartungen allerdings spürbar. Bloomberg-Redakteurin Natalie Lung hat Siri Recap und Live Rewind eine Woche lang genutzt und dabei auch Amazons Bee zum Vergleich herangezogen. Das rund 50 US-Dollar teure KI-Armband protokolliert Gespräche deutlich ausführlicher, während Apple die Inhalte radikal eindampft.**

## Quartalskonferenz in 16 Stichpunkten

Wie viel dabei laut [Test](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-17/apple-watch-siri-recap-review-ai-listening-adds-little-value) verloren geht, zeigt ausgerechnet Apples eigene Telefonkonferenz zu den Quartalszahlen. Siri Recap machte daraus 16 Stichpunkte. Das faltbare iPhone Duo kam darin nicht vor, ebenso wenig die mehrfach angesprochenen Lieferengpässe und Speicherpreise. Zahlen übernahm die KI zwar korrekt, oft fehlte aber der Bezug, um sie einzuordnen. Problematisch wurde es außerdem, wenn mehrere kurze Gespräche aufeinanderfolgten: Aussagen unterschiedlicher Kollegen landeten dann gemeinsam in einer Notiz. Da Apple Sprecher bewusst nicht zuordnet, lässt sich das im Nachhinein kaum entwirren. Auch Live Rewind, das per Doppeldruck auf die Digital Crown die letzten 15 Sekunden als Text anzeigt, patzte im Test bei der Erkennung, und zwar selbst in ruhiger Umgebung.

## Die Uhr hört auch am Nebentisch mit

Heikler ist ein anderer Punkt. Im Großraumbüro fasste Siri Recap auch Unterhaltungen zusammen, an denen die Testerin gar nicht beteiligt war. Bemerkt hat sie das erst später in der Siri-App. Live Rewind meldet sich beim Auslösen mit einem Signalton und einer Mikrofonanzeige, Siri Recap arbeitet dagegen ohne jeden Hinweis für das Umfeld. Apple betont, dass das Audiomaterial verschlüsselt über die Secure Exclave der Uhr an Private Cloud Compute geht und vollständige Aufnahmen nicht gespeichert werden. Zudem lässt sich die Funktion auf bestimmte Zeiten und Orte begrenzen. Sie pausiert außerdem, sobald bei AirPods oder Beats die Geräuschunterdrückung aktiv ist. Den Kollegen am Nebentisch hilft das allerdings wenig.

## Start im Dezember, aber nicht in der EU

Beide Funktionen stecken seit Anfang November in der Entwickler-Beta von watchOS 27.3 und setzen ein iPhone 16 oder neuer voraus. Die finale Version dürfte im Dezember zusammen mit iOS 27.3 erscheinen, das Beta-Label bleibt aber auch dann bestehen. Vorerst versteht Siri Recap nur Englisch. In der EU bleibt Audio Intelligence vorerst gesperrt, weil Siri AI hier wegen des Digital Markets Act noch nicht freigeschaltet ist. Einen Termin für den Start in Deutschland gibt es noch nicht.

items.articleBody:
As a librarian, I've worked with many government documents, some of which are odd. For example, I once encountered US Coast Guard instruction guide to emergency cold water survival that had an original publication format of microfiche.

[This manual](https://nre.tas.gov.au/Documents/Neil%20the%20Seal%20Management%20Plan.pdf) is similarly very specific, but the format is probably optimal. Neil the Seal is a south elephant seal who lives in Tasmania, Australia. He's six years old and weighs about 1 metric ton.

Neil is a popular tourist attraction, but also a wild animal and thus potentially dangerous. The Department of Natural Resources and Environment aims at peaceful co-existence between humans and Neil and thus has a risk assessment and response plan for "on-site seal management."

-via [@mikibosser](https://x.com/mikibosser/status/2122991714415825355)

items.articleBody:
There is always a catch. Or in the case of [Tesla](https://www.wired.com/tag/tesla/)’s self-driving [Cybercab](https://www.wired.com/story/tesla-cybercab-had-a-quiet-debut/), several.

Last Friday night, Tesla [said](https://x.com/robotaxi/status/2121384435241402737) it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs. The two-seat, gold vehicle is unlike any other on the market: It lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals, and is primarily driven by software. (Other autonomous vehicle companies, including Alphabet's [Waymo and](https://www.wired.com/tag/waymo/) Amazon’s [Zoox](https://www.wired.com/story/zoox-becomes-the-first-steering-wheel-free-robotaxi-to-charge-for-rides-in-the-us/), offer [self-driving rides on ride-hail networks](https://www.wired.com/tag/robotaxis/), but don’t let people buy their cars.) Tesla’s "[limited release](https://x.com/robotaxi/status/2121384438496190523)” will supposedly offer some people (unclear how many) the opportunity to pay $29,900 to take delivery in December.

From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/cars/2026/11/tesla-will-sell-you-a-cybercab-for-30000-then-charge-299-a-month-to-use-it/)

## Thomann Cyber Deals

Die Cyber Deals bei Thomann sind noch lange nicht vorbei. Bis zum 30.11.2026 könnt ihr weiterhin kräftig sparen. Es lohnt sich also, die Angebote genauer unter die Lupe zu nehmen. Im Bereich Synthesizer sind jetzt sogar noch einige neue Deals hinzugekommen, die wir euch hier vorstellen. Schaut auch regelmäßig auf der Thomann-Website vorbei, damit euch kein Angebot entgeht!

Endlich ist es wieder so weit! Wie jedes Jahr präsentiert Thomann die Cyber Deals, die ab heute bis einschließlich **30. November 2026, 23:59 Uhr,** erhältlich sind!

Jetzt lohnt es sich zuzuschlagen! Wie wäre es mit dem lang ersehnten Instrument oder einem musikalischen Geschenk zu Weihnachten: Mit Rabatten von bis zu 70 Prozent bieten die [Thomann Cyber Deals](https://www.thomann.de/intl/special_cyber-deals.html) die perfekte Gelegenheit, um musikalische Wünsche wahr werden zu lassen.

## Cyber Deals: Synthesizer, Grooveboxen und mehr Cyber Deals

Selbstverständlich hat Thomann auch an die Synthesizer gedacht, und wir haben es uns nicht nehmen lassen, euch einige ausgewählte Deals vorzustellen. Ob Sound-Designer, Klangschrauber, Beat-Produzenten, Bedroom-Producer: Ihr werdet sicher einen guten Deal finden!

Wir empfehlen euch aber dringend, auch die [Thomann Cyber Deals](https://www.thomann.de/intl/special_cyber-deals.html)-Website zu besuchen und die Angebote in Ruhe zu durchstöbern.

Mit dabei sind zahlreiche Top-Marken aus unterschiedlichsten Kategorien, darunter Akai, Behringer, Beyerdynamic, Epiphone, Focusrite, Gibson, Harley Benton, JBL, Martin Guitar, Millenium, PRS, Sennheiser, Shure und Yamaha.

**Wer die Thomann Cyber Deals nicht verpassen möchte, sollte schnell sein: Die besten Angebote können rasch vergriffen sein: Hier geht es zu den [Deals.](https://www.thomann.de/intl/special_cyber-deals.html)**

## Roland TR-1000 und Thon Case Roland TR-1000

Mit der TR-1000 hat Roland eine echte State of the Art Drum-Machine auf den Markt gebracht, die all die interessanten Features vereint, welche die legendären Roland Drum Machines TR-808, TR-909 und weitere Klassiker berühmt gemacht haben. Die TR-1000 verfügt über eine analoge und eine digitale Klangerzeugung. Außerdem kann sie mithilfe der VA-Synthese Bass- und Synthesizer-Sounds erzeugen und auch sampeln.

**Der Preis der Roland TR-1000 bleibt während der Cyber Deals unverändert bei 2.699,00 Euro. Thomann legt euch allerdings das passende Thon Case Roland TR-1000 kostenlos dazu, für das normalerweise weitere 225,00 Euro fällig werden. Dabei handelt es sich um ein maßgeschneidertes Case für die TR-1000, das auch für den Tournee-Einsatz ausgelegt ist.**

Hier geht es zum [Roland TR-1000 Test](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/roland-tr-1000-test/)

## Arturia AstroLab 61 Silver

Die Arturia AstroLab Serie erlaubt es, Sounds aus der Arturia V-Collection Software im AstroLab zu synthetisieren. So benötigt ihr auf der Bühne keinen Computer mehr und könnt euch ganz auf das Musizieren konzentrieren.

Während der Cyber Days gibt es das Arturia AstroLab 61 Silver verbilligt. Wie der Name sagt, wird es mit 61 Tasten und in der Farbe Silber ausgeliefert. Es gibt 11 Prozent Rabatt, und das bedeutet, ihr müsst nur 1279,00 Euro anstatt 1430,00 Euro bezahlen.

Hier geht es zum [Arturia AstroLab Test.](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/arturia-astrolab-88-test/)

## Moog Muse

Der Moog Muse ist der neue Polyphone analoge Synthesizer von Moog mit 8 Stimmen, 61 Tasten und vielfältigen Sounddesign-Möglichkeiten, die keine Wünsche offen lassen. Während der Cyber Deals gibt es den analogen Synthesizer mit **17 Prozent Rabatt.** **Normalerweise kostet er 3499,00 Euro**, aber während der Cyber Deals müsst ihr nur**2897,00 Euro** auf den Tisch legen.

[Hier geht es zum Moog Muse Test](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/moog-muse-test/)

hier geht es zum [Novation Launchpad Pro MK3 Test.](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/novation-launchpad-pro-mk3-test/)

hier geht es zum [Ableton Push 3 Test.](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/ableton-push-3-test/)

## Erica Synths Steampipe

Erica Synths Steampipe ist ein achtstimmiger Physical Modeling Desktop Synthesizer. Er verfügt über 32 Parameter und fünf LFOs.

Normalerweise wird dieser Synthesizer für 1.099,00 Euro angeboten. Doch jetzt könnt ihr diesen experimentellen Synthesizer für **899,00 Euro**bekommen. Das entspricht einer**Ersparnis von 200,00 Euro.**

[Hier geht es zum Erica Synths Steampipe Test.](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/erica-synths-steampipe-test/)

## 1010music Bento

Das ist ein echtes Highlight: Thomann reduziert die 1010music Bento Groovebox von 909,00 Euro auf attraktive **799,00 Euro**. Eine gute Gelegenheit, sich die vielseitige Groovebox zu einem deutlich günstigeren Preis zu sichern.

[Hier geht es zum 1010music Bento Test.](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/test-1010music-bento-beyond-the-blackbox/)

## SOMA Flux

Ein außergewöhnliches Instrument ist auch SOMA Flux. Der digitale Synthesizer verfügt über eine magnetische Tastatur mit 37 Noten und kann je nach ausgewähltem Algorithmus ein bis zwölf Stimmen erzeugen. Das stabförmige Instrument ist ein echter Hingucker und lässt sich auch auf der Bühne umschnallen oder in der Hand halten. Damit zieht ihr garantiert alle Blicke auf euch.

Während der Thomann Cyber Deals gibt es SOMA Flux für **888,00 Euro**anstatt 1.199,00 Euro. Das ist eine**Ersparnis von 311,00 Euro.**

## Akai MPC XL

Bei der Akai MPC XL handelt es sich um die neueste Generation, die im Januar 2026 erschienen ist. Auch sie könnt ihr während der Cyber Deals günstiger erwerben. Das Flaggschiff der MPC-Serie verfügt über 16 GB RAM und 256 GB internen Speicher. Die MPC Pads wurden mit der neuesten 3D-Sensortechnologie ausgestattet. Und noch vieles mehr!

Normalerweise müsst ihr 2.435,00 Euro für die Akai MPC XL zahlen. Doch jetzt habt ihr die Gelegenheit, diese Powerworkstation für nur **2.199,00 Euro**zu erwerben. Das entspricht einer**Ersparnis von 236,00 Euro.**

[Hier geht es zum Akai MPC XL Test.](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/akai-professional-mpc-xl-test/)

Der Yamaha SEQTRAK ist ebenfalls Teil der Thomann Cyber Deals. Die vielseitige Groovebox vereint Synthesizer, Drumcomputer, Sampler und Visuals in einem kompakten Gerät und eignet sich hervorragend für die mobile Musikproduktion. Thomann bietet den SEQTRAK in Black oder Orange jeweils für **229,00 Euro**statt 359,00 Euro an. Das entspricht einer**Ersparnis von 130,00 Euro.**

[Hier geht es zum Yamaha SEQTRAK Test.](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/yamaha-seqtrak-test/)

Auch Technofans kommen bei den Thomann Cyber Deals auf ihre Kosten. Gleich zwei Geräte laden dazu ein Acid und Techno Tracks zu produzieren: Die RD-6-TG Drummachine basiert auf der Roland TR-606. Den passenden Acid Bass Sound steuert die TD-3-TG bei, Behringers Interpretation der legendären Roland TB-303. Beide Geräte gibt es in einem orangenen transparenten Gehäuse. Partnerlook!

Bei Thomann bekommt ihr die **RD-6-TG**jetzt für**89,00 Euro**statt 109,00 Euro und die**TD-3-TG**für**79,00 Euro**statt 95,00 Euro. Im Set zahlt ihr also nur**168,00 Euro anstatt 204,00 Euro.**

Im Rahmen der Thomann Cyber Deals ist das Instrument jetzt für **399,00 Euro anstatt 439,00 Euro** erhältlich.

items.articleBody:
Links links links…

- [Grand Theft Auto VI will be depraved](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/opinion/grand-theft-auto-danger-art.html?) — but “banning art has never been convincingly shown to halt society’s depravity,” writes Daisy Dixon. Better to let it spur us to “consider what it says about our own worst impulses”
- [“The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice,” MLK famously said](https://liberalism.org/essays/the-perils-of-believing-in-progress) — What does that mean, exactly? Jacob Levy on how to best interpret ideas of human progress (scroll to bottom for audio)
- [“Social institutions can raise the production and use of knowledge by broadening access to intellectual exchange beyond formal academic networks”](https://www.monirbounadi.com/Bounadi_JMP.pdf) — how cafes contributed to the rise of science (via MR)
- [“Our sense of beauty is a wonderfully positive trait in us because it’s never going to be quite satisfied”](https://thereader.mitpress.mit.edu/beauty-is-everywhere-but-what-is-it-for/) — an interview with Nicholas Humphrey on why the world is so beautiful
- [Aristotle and the Fielder Method](https://theconversation.com/how-aristotle-helps-us-unpack-the-art-of-deception-in-nathan-fielders-you-can-see-everything-295602) — John Robert Hacker-Wright on “You Can See Everything” and the distinction between action and imitation
- [Text by Karl Marx. Illustrations by Richard Scarry.](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dco27Hvk_KP) — from Zach Mander. [More here](https://www.instagram.com/p/DcrbyLxE-8q).
- [“Why do I want myself in particular to exist in ten years?”](https://schwitzsplinters.blogspot.com/2026/11/why-do-i-want-myself-in-particular-to.html) — Eric Schwitzgebel, recently diagnosed with metastatic kidney cancer, ponders the question

items.articleBody:
**Wenn Knochen nachwächst, kann er seine äußere Form zurückerlangen, bevor seine innere Struktur ausgereift ist. An regenerierenden Zehenspitzen von Mäusen war die grobe Knochenstruktur nach rund drei Wochen wiederhergestellt, während sich die lokale Steifigkeit mindestens eine weitere Woche veränderte. Der Befund zeigt, warum die sichtbare Regeneration allein noch nichts über die vollständige mechanische Erholung aussagt.**

**College Station (U.S.A.).** Bei vielen Säugetieren wachsen größere verlorene Gliedmaßenteile nicht wieder nach. Unter bestimmten Bedingungen können sich aber die äußersten Bereiche von Fingern und Zehen regenerieren, einschließlich des dortigen Knochens und weiterer Gewebe. Unklar war bisher, ob die wiederhergestellte Form auch bedeutet, dass das neu gebildete Knochengewebe bereits mechanisch ausgereift ist.

Nach einer Amputation wird zunächst ein Teil des verbliebenen Knochens abgebaut. Anschließend bildet sich ein sogenanntes Blastem, eine Ansammlung von Zellen, die sich vermehren und zu unterschiedlichen Gewebetypen entwickeln können. Daraus entstehen neue Strukturen, deren innere Organisation und lokale Steifigkeit sich während des Nachwachsens verändern.

### Form und Steifigkeit getrennt untersucht

Forscher der Texas A&M University um Dr. Yuxiao Zhou haben nun die Regeneration der Endglieder von Mäusezehen in mehreren Größenordnungen untersucht. Dazu kombinierten sie wiederholte Mikro-Computertomografien mit Rasterkraftmikroskopie an entnommenen Gewebeproben und Computermodellen, die die Verteilung mechanischer Spannungen und Verformungen berechnen.

Für die mikroskopischen Steifigkeitsmessungen wurden zu jedem Untersuchungszeitpunkt Proben von vier verschiedenen Mäusen ausgewertet. Die Simulationen beruhten auf tomografischen Datensätzen von fünf Zehen je Zeitpunkt und ergänzten die lokalen Messungen durch eine Betrachtung der gesamten Knochenstruktur. Beide Datensätze stammten aus unterschiedlichen Tiergruppen und konnten deshalb nicht an denselben Zehen unmittelbar miteinander korreliert werden.

> „Das Computermodell bildet das Verhalten der gesamten Zehe ab, während die Rasterkraftmikroskopie die Mikrostruktur der Gewebe sichtbar macht. Den Zusammenhang zwischen diesen beiden Bereichen zu erklären, war sehr wichtig und sehr anspruchsvoll“, erklärt Hanwen Fan von der Texas A&M University.

### Die Form ist schneller zurück als die Steifigkeit

Zu Beginn der Regeneration fanden sich im Blastem noch weiche, ungeordnete Gewebebereiche mit einzelnen steiferen Zonen. Im neu entstehenden Knochen bildeten sich kleine mineralisierte Bereiche, die allmählich wuchsen und miteinander verschmolzen. Am verbliebenen Knochenstumpf lief gleichzeitig ein eigener Umbauprozess ab, der sich von der Neubildung an der Zehenspitze unterschied.

Nach 21 Tagen war die grobe anatomische Kontinuität des Zehenknochens wiederhergestellt. Die Rasterkraftmikroskopie zeigte aber, dass der neu entstandene Bereich an der Spitze noch deutlich nachgiebiger war als der näher am Körper gelegene Knochen. Erst am 28. Tag erreichte seine lokal gemessene Steifigkeit in den untersuchten Bereichen annähernd die Werte des verbliebenen Knochens, obwohl Unterschiede zum unverletzten Ausgangszustand bestanden.

> „Obwohl die äußere Form fast wiederhergestellt ist, reift die Mikrostruktur weiter. Selbst nachdem die Form wiederhergestellt wurde, bauen die Knochenzellen im Mikro- und Nanomaßstab noch aktiv eine robustere Struktur auf“, erklärt Dr. Yuxiao Zhou.

Die Untersuchung macht damit zwei unterschiedliche Zeitverläufe sichtbar. Die äußere Rekonstruktion war bereits weit fortgeschritten, als die innere Anordnung der Knochenmatrix und ihre mechanischen Eigenschaften noch Veränderungen durchliefen.

### Belastung verteilt sich zunehmend gleichmäßiger

Auch die Computermodelle zeigten, dass sich die mechanischen Bedingungen während der Regeneration verändern. Sie ergaben sieben Tage nach der Amputation für die Belastungsunterschiede zwischen Zehenunterseite und Oberseite ein Verhältnis von etwa 3,9 bei den Spannungen und 3,8 bei den Verformungen. Bis zum 31. Tag näherten sich beide Verhältnisse dem Wert eins, der einer annähernd ausgeglichenen Verteilung wie beim unverletzten Knochen entspricht.

> „Unsere Hypothese ist, dass das Ungleichgewicht nach der Verletzung einer der Faktoren sein könnte, die den Prozess antreiben, sodass die Zehe ihre ursprüngliche mechanische Umgebung wiedererlangen kann“, erklärt Dr. Yuxiao Zhou.

Diese mögliche Steuerungswirkung ist allerdings eine Hypothese und wurde durch die Modellrechnungen nicht als Ursache nachgewiesen. Die Simulationen verwendeten vereinfachte, nahezu statische Belastungen und unterschiedliche Angriffspunkte der Kräfte je nach Regenerationsstadium. Die berechneten Spannungen lassen sich daher nicht mit einer tatsächlich gemessenen Gehbewegung oder einer direkt getesteten Belastbarkeit gleichsetzen.

### Noch keine Aussage über die Funktion im Alltag

Die Arbeit untersuchte ausschließlich acht Wochen alte weibliche Mäuse und umfasste bei den lokalen Messungen nur vier unabhängige Tiere je Zeitpunkt. Ob die beobachteten Zeitverläufe auch für männliche Tiere, andere Altersgruppen oder menschliche Verletzungen gelten, bleibt offen. Zudem wurde weder die Gehfähigkeit noch die tatsächliche Belastung der regenerierten Zehen im Alltag gemessen.

Für die regenerative Medizin ist der Befund dennoch relevant, weil neu gebildeter Knochen nicht allein nach seiner sichtbaren Form beurteilt werden sollte. Künftige Untersuchungen müssen klären, wie die lokale Reifung, die Kräfte im Gewebe und die wirkliche Funktion zusammenhängen. Eine Behandlung zur verbesserten Knochenregeneration beim Menschen wurde mit dieser Studie nicht entwickelt oder erprobt.

items.articleBody:
The end of the year is quickly approaching, and you know what that means: gifting season is here.

Like clockwork, we’re back with a carefully curated, handy dandy [gift guide](https://colossal.shop/pages/2026-gift-guide) to help you pick out the perfect presents for each name on your list. Organized by passions and personalities, our list has something special for everyone. So sit back, brew a cup of tea, and get scrolling! You’re about to have the breeziest holiday shopping yet.

As always, thank you for supporting Colossal.

**For the Creative Professional**

Visual thinkers understand the absolute joy of [impeccably designed things](https://colossal.shop/collections/for-the-creative-professional). Treat the creative in your life to studio essentials that make the workday lighter and intriguing reads to keep the ideas flowing.

**For the Maximalist**

More is more! If bold colors, clashing patterns, and whimsical graphics are that special someone’s vibe, we’ve got the [perfect accessories](https://colossal.shop/collections/for-the-maximalist-1) to complete their closet.

**For the Nature Lover**

We all know someone who feels the happiest among flora, fauna, and the great outdoors. Bring [a bit of nature](https://colossal.shop/collections/for-the-nature-lover) to them with a new pair of gardening gloves, fungi-inspired decor and puzzles, a guide to foraging for handmade inks, and plenty more.

**For the Tasteful Host**

Those with great taste often have a cozy home to match. Help your favorite host make their space even warmer with [aesthetically-pleasing objects](https://colossal.shop/collections/for-the-tasteful-host) for cooking, gathering, and lingering just a bit longer.

**For the Serial Hobbyist**

Our exciting range of craft kits open up a world of possibilities for those who never seem to get tired of [trying new hobbies](https://colossal.shop/collections/for-the-serial-hobbyist). From hand loom weaving and embroidery to pressing flowers and growing herbs, there’s something new to try for everyone.

**For the Budding Artist**

What’s more important than encouraging those just beginning to explore their creative side? Surprise that [little one](https://colossal.shop/collections/for-the-budding-artist) with a big imagination with specially-crafted wooden toys, beautiful books, unique crayons, and beyond.

Find more in the [Colossal Shop](https://colossal.shop).

Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a [Colossal Member](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/members) today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. items.articleBody:
[Homer’s Greeks had no inner life](https://iai.tv/articles/homers-greeks-had-no-inner-life-auid-3724). That’s the title of a recent introduction to Julian Jaynes’s bicameral theory of mind. To recap: in [The Origin of Consciousness in the Breakdown of the Bicameral Mind](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0618057072), Jaynes argued that intelligent behavior preceded introspective consciousness. People could speak, learn, farm, build cities, and solve problems without mentally representing themselves as an “I” deliberating within an internal world.

In Jaynes’s theory, routine behavior followed habit but difficult or unfamiliar situations triggered “command hallucinations,” voices experienced as gods, ancestors, or rulers giving instructions. One part of the mind issued commands; another obeyed—hence “bicameral.” Increasing complexity, migration, and the breakdown of established authority undermined the bicameral mind. Starting around 1200 BC, roughly between the Iliad and the Odyssey, people increasingly began imagining alternatives and narrating their own actions within an internal mental space, in short, they became conscious. Consciousness was thus not a biological given but a product of cultural and linguistic evolution.

I used to dismiss Jaynes’s theory completely, The idea of otherwise normal but unconscious human beings seemed absurd. Today, I am not so sure. If you think AIs are not conscious, then a central premise of Jaynes’s theory becomes much more plausible: namely, a civilization of thinking, talking doing, but unconscious beings. The AIs are an existence proof. That said, I still find the evidence for a sharp break around the Homeric era weak. Linguistic differences between the *Iliad* and later texts are a weak reed for such a big claim and can be explained in other ways. The case for a near-universal transition in a few centuries is thin. On Occam’s-razor grounds I favor continuity. The fact that some animals appear conscious pushes in the same direction.

AIs also undermine Jaynes’s theory in one way. Jaynes bases part of his theory on a change in the way people spoke—moving from describing their actions in terms of following commands to describing their actions in terms of deliberation and “I.” But if AIs are not conscious, then non-conscious beings can describe what they are doing in conscious terms. Of course, AIs have human culture as a foundation, which the early non-conscious humans would not have had, so I don’t think this is a strong hit on the theory.

Still, Jaynes’s theory is that until very recently most humans lacked introspective consciousness. Does this mean that they couldn’t suffer or didn’t deserve moral consideration? I would think not, but it raises the question of *what kind of consciousness* are we looking for in AIs? Are AIs as conscious as Jaynes’s Achilles? If we can debate whether Homeric era humans were conscious, it’s no surprise that we have difficulty deciding whether AIs are or could be conscious.

In [What Did We Learn from Torturing Babies](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2025/03/what-do-we-learn-from-torturing-babies.html) I wrote about the era when doubts about babies’ capacity to feel pain helped justify surgery without anesthesia. Babies certainly behaved *as if* they felt pain, but a theory overrode the plain observations. That seems crazy if you take behavior seriously as evidence of experience—a broad Turing-test approach. But taking that approach seriously also suggests AIs might well be conscious.

Ultimately, the issue is not whether Jaynes was right or wrong but the fact that there is any debate at all is telling. We don’t have a good test for consciousness whether applied to the past, to other animals, or to machines. If we are unsure whether Achilles had an inner life perhaps we should be unsure whether Claude has an inner life.

items.articleBody:
**[Joe Bonamassa](https://www.gearnews.de/gear-von-joe-bonamassa/)ist ein Umtriebiger. Nicht nur musikalisch spielt er auf vielen Schauplätzen, auch bei seinen Signature-Modellen zusammen mit Gibson und Epiphone erscheinen laufend neue Modelle. Heute stellen wir euch die Joe Bonamassa Skinnerburst vor. Dieses limitierte Modell von Epiphone basiert auf seiner legendären ’59 Les Paul Standard**.

## Epiphone und Bonamassa

Bonamassa und Epiphone, das Kapitel hat für Fans der Blueslegende in den letzten zwei Jahrzehnten laufend Neues hervorgebracht. Allein **neun** Signature-Modelle konnte ich auf Gearnews zählen, unter anderem eine [1963 SG](https://www.gearnews.de/epiphone-joe-bonamassa-1963-sg-custom/), eine[ES-335](https://www.gearnews.de/epiphone-joe-bonamassa-es-355-sie-ist-endlich-da/) und eine [Flying V.](https://www.gearnews.de/epiphone-baut-die-1958-amos-flying-v-fuer-joe-bonamassa/)

Da reiht sich die Skinnerburst perfekt ein. Von besagtem Modell gab es bereits 2014 mal einen Limited Run, jetzt können Paula-Fans und Bonamassa-Jünger die „Direktor Skinner“-Gitarre auch für kleineres Geld zu sich nach Hause holen.

## Joe Bonamassa Skinnerburst

Limitiert ist auch die Joe Bonamassa Skinnerburst, sprich, wenn das, was da ist, weg ist, gibt es (erstmal) keinen Nachschub. Bei der Skinnerburst sticht zuerst die Farbgebung ins Auge, die für die Namensgebung nach dem Schuldirektor der Grundschule in Springfield gesorgt hat.

Epiphone Joe Bonamassa Skinnerburst · Quelle: Epiphone

„Dirty Lemon“ vorne, „Faded Cherry“ hinten. Mahagonikorpus samt Decke aus Ahorn mit Riegelahornfurnier, eingeleimter Mahagonihals (Custom-59-Rounded-C-Profil), Palisandergriffbrett, Graph-Tech-Sattel: Wo Epiphone draufsteht, ist bei Les Pauls sehr häufig diese Holzausstattung drin.

Auf dem Griffbrett finden wir 22 Medium-Jumbo-Bünde, Perloid-Trapezoid-Inlays und am Headstock (Kalamazoo-Form) Deluxe-Mechaniken von Epiphone.

## ProBucker und LockTone

Bleiben wir bei der Hardware der Joe Bonamassa Skinnerburst. Bei der Bridge kommt hier eine vom Typ LockTone Tune-o-Matic zum Einsatz. Seitens der Pickups kommt die Signature mit zwei ProBucker-Tonabnehmern, einem Probucker Custom am Steg, sowie einem ProBucker 3 am Hals.

Zwei ProBucker und die LockTone-Bridge · Quelle: Epiphone

Bei der Elektronik hält man sich nah an das legendären 59er-Vorbild. Epiphone verbaut CTS-Potis und Mallory-Kondensatoren. Bei der Verteilung ist alles wie immer: zwei Volume- und zwei Tone-Regler, dazu ein 3-Wege-Schalter.

## Was kostet die Epiphone Joe Bonamassa Skinnerburst?

Ihr bekommt die Epiphone Joe Bonamassa Skinnerburst ab sofort für **1.069,- Euro** [bei Thomann*](https://www.thomann.de/de/epiphone_bonamassa_59_les_paul_dl.htm?offid=1&affid=84). Ein Hartschalenkoffer samt Nerdville-Logo liegt bei.

items.articleBody:
When Keisha Lance Bottoms, the next governor of Georgia, announced her transition team, one name in particular stood out: Tyler Perry, the filmmaker most famous for playing Madea, a Black matriarch who puffs on cigarettes and disciplines smart-aleck children, and who can draw out a “hello” with so many southern syllables that it sounds like “hallelujah.”

Perry’s movies may be frowned upon, especially by members of the Black elite. Some people thought Bottoms’s pick was in poor taste (or, as one *New York* magazine writer put it, [“unserious”](https://nymag.com/intelligencer/article/black-governors-byron-donalds-keisha-lance-bottom-black-firsts-trap.html)). But others—myself included—were here for it. Many working-class, southern, and older Black people love Perry, and he’s always stayed true to that audience. Bottoms’s choice was another way that she’s leaned into her Blackness. Her father was an R&B and soul singer, and her mother had multiple jobs, including one in a hair salon. On [Bottoms’s website](https://keishalancebottoms.com/) are photos of her wearing golden box braids with her edges laid. This may not mean anything to most Americans, but to Black women, it means she’s connected to us by the hours and hours we have spent sitting in a salon chair getting our hair tugged, parted, and braided, the ends dipped in boiling water. One Christmas, when she was the mayor of Atlanta, she posted a photo of her mac and cheese and the words: “[Trust, nothing dry here](https://x.com/KeishaBottoms/status/1077677720719511557?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw%7Ctwcamp%5Etweetembed%7Ctwterm%5E1077677720719511557%7Ctwgr%5E38603882cfc876e3d81801331f8de01344655d93%7Ctwcon%5Es1_&ref_url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.kcra.com%2Farticle%2Fmayor-defends-mac-and-cheese-recipe-after-posting-photo-to-social-media%2F25682842).” The day before the midterms, she visited the grave of her great-great-grandmother, Betsy Peek, who was born into slavery.

The midterms didn’t just result in the election of a record number of Black governors—four, bringing the total nationwide to five—and two new Black senators. Many of the politicians themselves seem, like Bottoms, to be unapologetically embracing their Blackness, and their southernness, in a new way.

Randall Woodfin has been mayor of Birmingham, Alabama, since 2017, but this election seems to have brought out a different side of him. Google him: There he is wearing a tailored suit jacket with a milky-white collared shirt. But on Election Day, he posted a photo of himself flaunting a sunset-gold grill that spelled out the words: Go Vote. In the caption, he wrote, “Ice on the grill, sticker on the chest. Election Day is Today.” I don’t think I’ve ever seen someone with grillz in a professional setting before. What I saw in the photo was a Black politician saying you don’t always have to mute the Blackest parts of yourself.

*[[Adam Serwer: Scott Colom is Mississippi’s first Black senator in 150 years](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/11/scott-colom-us-senate-democrats/689395/?utm_source=feed)]*

Ashley Etienne served as the director of communications for President Obama’s Cabinet and in the same role later for Vice President Harris. When Obama was running, Etienne told me, he was pressured to “rise above” his Blackness and discouraged from “overly identifying as being Black.” (Though sometimes, she said, he “couldn’t help himself.” She remembered a moment during the 2008 race when he addressed some of Hillary Clinton’s criticisms of him: “When you’re running for presidency, you gotta …” and he mimicked Jay-Z’s “Dirt Off Your Shoulder” gesture.)

She lamented what she saw as the pressure on Harris to be “a buttoned-up kind of politician.” She recalled, on one conference call, asking the vice president’s team how the day was going. The chief of staff responded, “Today is a good day.” Without missing a beat, Harris said, “I didn’t even have to use my AK”—a lyric from Ice Cube’s “It Was a Good Day.” In the moment, Etienne said, she thought to herself, “If only I could get her to be this person in public, that would really transform things for her.” Etienne told me that she was glad to see that many of the Black politicians who won in the midterms seem freer to break with narrow expectations about how Black politicians are meant to behave.

The shift isn’t just about race, but also about class. The new Black politicians didn’t all go to elite universities, in contrast to earlier figures such as Obama (Columbia and Harvard), Cory Booker (Stanford and Oxford), and Deval Patrick (Harvard and Harvard). Many went to state universities or historically Black schools. Bottoms went to Florida A&M University; Byron Donalds, the Republican who will be Florida’s first Black governor, went to FAMU and Florida State. Woodfin went to Morehouse College. Juliana Stratton, the new senator from Illinois, went to the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, and to DePaul University for law school. Scott Colom, the first Black senator from Mississippi in 150 years, attended Millsaps College and the University of Wisconsin Law School.

Some of these politicians seem more comfortable acting working-class in a way that might once have been considered crude. Colom—the first Black senator from Mississippi in 150 years—originally gained a lot of attention for his “pick another protein” ad. The commercial taunted his opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, for replying to a question about the price of beef with a recommendation that Mississippians buy something else instead. The commercial features three different types of voters. First, a white man tells the camera, “Pick another protein? Shiiiii—I’d rather pick another senator instead,” while flipping burgers on a grill. Then a Black woman taking a bite of fried fish from a Styrofoam plate says, “Pick another protein? She done lost her damn mind. I’d rather pick another senator.” Lastly, a white woman opens the glass door of a convenience-store freezer while saying, “Pick another protein? What the f—”

It was crass, and people loved it, because it captured their genuine frustration. Colom has been known to wear a hoodie, jeans, and sneakers to a press conference, and he doesn’t try to hide his deep southern accent. “He speaks Mississippi,” as one of my friends from the state put it.

A month before the midterms, President Trump was in Mississippi at a campaign rally for Hyde-Smith when he mentioned Colom. He asked the crowd, “How the hell do you say that guy’s name? What a name.”

People have had questions about my name before. When I was a young journalist, a white colleague who couldn’t pronounce “Jenisha,” and didn’t care to try, asked, “Do you mind if I just call you Jen?” Another person would jokingly call me Khadijah, while another admitted not wanting to mess with me because of my last name, which reminded her of the Watts riots in L.A. Colom’s team turned this attack into another successful ad, in which you hear his name repeated by news anchors, Obama, and finally Trump himself. Colom pops back on-screen to say: “He got that right.”

*[[Adam Serwer: Even where MAGA won, MAGA lost](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/11/maga-party-demographic-shift/689286/?utm_source=feed)]*

In a funny way, this shift among Black politicians may owe something to the current president. Trump has broken American ethics, norms, and even laws with his outrageous and cruel behavior. But originally, he gained support by appearing to be unapologetically, authentically himself. He valued relatability more than decorum, and many voters wanted that. To put it another way: He killed respectability politics. “Before him, there was a prototype, and everybody had to fit into the box. And Trump blew that thing out of the water,” Etienne said. The shift has allowed politicians to “embrace culture, embrace their own identity” and use that to “turn out voters.”

Charmion Kinder, who was a senior adviser to Vice President Harris and a White House press aide to First Lady Michelle Obama, made a similar point. “If I were to give him credit for anything, it would be authenticity,” she told me. But she pointed out that these winning Black candidates also understood their audience and were intentional about engaging with Americans who traditionally always show up to vote. Candidates started “talking to people in their language,” she said.

After the Trump administration has spent years attacking Black history and DEI initiatives and trying to purge Black people from positions of power in the government and the military, it would be a pleasing irony if Black politicians ended up being liberated, in this particular way, by his norm-destroying legacy. Black people are not a monolith—and Black politicians shouldn’t have to be either.

items.title: What does it mean to be “laser-focused on affordability”?
items.subtitle: Hakeem Jeffries addresses supporters at an election night event in Washington, D.C., after Democrats won the House on November 3, 2026.
items.feedText: As a naturally disputatious person, I was a little bit annoyed by how good the vibes were at last week’s “What’s Next” conference from the Majority Democrats. Annoyed in particular because I suspect that many of the Democrats who believe they’ve reached consensus around ideas like Democrats need to be “laser-focused on affordability” don’t actually agree with each other. Or, rather, that what they have agreed upon is a slogan rather than a plan. Words are, after…
items.articleBody:
As a naturally disputatious person, I was a little bit annoyed by how good the vibes were at last week’s “What’s Next” conference from the Majority Democrats. Annoyed in particular because I suspect that many of the Democrats who believe they’ve reached consensus around ideas like [Democrats need to be “laser-focused on affordability”](https://www.google.com/search?q=%22laser-focused+on+affordability%22&oq=%22laser-focused+on+affordability%22&gs_lcrp=EgZjaHJvbWUyBggAEEUYOTIHCAEQIRigATIHCAIQIRirAjIHCAMQIRiPAjIHCAQQIRiPAtIBCDI5OTNqMGo3qAIAsAIA&sourceid=chrome&source=chrome.ob&ie=UTF-8) don’t actually agree with each other.

Or, rather, that what they have agreed upon is a slogan rather than a plan.

Words are, after all, tricky things and full of different kinds of ambiguities that clever sloganeers exploit. The way that politics works is that participants in political debates talk about highly technical policy areas while simultaneously trying to [communicate with normal people](https://www.slowboring.com/p/democrats-next-challenge-talk-like) who are not versed in technical jargon.

Doing this effectively is a real skill. But a lot of the skill resides precisely in *not* being clear about exactly what you mean.

For example, back in John Fetterman’s 2022 campaign, when he was a progressive hero, he used to say that he was determined to “[make more shit in America](https://www.commondreams.org/news/2022/07/13/after-latest-inflation-figures-fetterman-slams-corporate-execs-raising-prices-us)” as part of his solution to inflation. Part of what made this turn of phrase so good is that it’s ambiguous between an abundance-flavored agenda of supply-side reforms and a protectionist agenda of tariffs. If a writer turned in a piece to me that was ambiguous in that way, I’d ask them to try to be clearer about what they’re saying. But in politics, it’s *good* to be unclear. And while obviously Fetterman has fallen out of favor with the left, the consultants behind him also worked on the Zohran Mamdani, Graham Platner, and Abdul El-Sayed races and continue to be quite skilled and influential, not least in popularizing “affordability” as an alternative to “inflation.”

What’s good about this term, though, is precisely that it’s less clear.

In a campaign speech or ad, it’s optimal to find terms that resonate with large groups of people while being vague in their specific implications. But if you’re trying to reach consensus on a policy agenda, you need to actually work through the disagreement, not find turns of phrase that cleverly paper over it.

#### Multiple approaches to affordability

If we took the term “affordability” literally, I think it would mean something like what economists call “real income.” In America, for example, cars are broadly affordable — [it’s more common for a family to own two cars than to own zero](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/11/14/1-in-10-americans-rarely-or-never-drive-a-car/?trk=public_post_comment-text&utm_source=chatgpt.com#:~:text=Nationally%2C%208%25%20of%20households%20don%E2%80%99t%20have%20a%20vehicle%2C%20a%20third%20have%20one%20car%20available%20and%2036%25%20have%20two%20cars.%20Another%2022%25%20of%20households%20have%20three%20or%20more%20vehicles.) — even though cars are expensive. Incomes are high enough that people can afford them. And, indeed, Americans of 2026 can afford more (and better) cars than they could afford in 1986 or 1956. In India, by contrast, incomes are low, so [most people can’t afford cars](https://thewire.in/economy/most-indians-cant-even-afford-entry-level-cars-maruti-suzuki-chairman-explained-why).

This definition has two virtues. One, I think, is that it makes a lot of sense as a question of technical economics. Would you prefer a world where you earn $250,000 and a burrito costs $20 or a world where you earn $65,000 and a burrito costs $9? Rationally, it’s clearly better to be in the former world.

The other is that in terms of progressive politics, “affordability as real income” lends itself to some obvious policy fixes.

[↗ slowboring.com](https://www.slowboring.com/p/what-does-it-mean-to-be-laser-focused)

On a balmy night in 2019, 35-year-old Barakat was on his way home, driven by friends through the ancient, mountainous Syrian village of Barisha, one among the previously abandoned Byzantine “Dead Cities.”

“I was with my best friends. They wanted to drop me off at home,” the father of five later [told](https://www.npr.org/2019/12/03/784553329/syrians-say-innocent-civilians-were-killed-in-u-s-raid-on-abu-bakr-al-baghdadi?t=1583770935798&t=1583840994461) NPR. Barakat and his two companions had finished their day’s work as agricultural laborers at an olive press. “We had pumpkin seeds and bought coffee on the road and were having fun.”

Unknown to them, a fateful military operation was occurring nearby. Three hundred meters away, a team of U.S. special forces was raiding the compound of Islamic State leader [Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi](https://theintercept.com/2019/11/10/baghdadi-death-war-on-terror/).

As the attack unfolded, most U.S. surveillance and reconnaissance assets were trained on the compound itself. Yet, known to few at the time, a new set of artificial eyes had been introduced to U.S. warfare in Iraq and Syria. Computer vision target detection, part of the [Pentagon’s algorithmic warfare program known as Project Maven](https://theintercept.com/2019/03/09/anduril-industries-project-maven-palmer-luckey/), enabled the military to recognize enemy personnel and vehicles through AI-assisted fusion and analysis of images and video.

As Barakat’s vehicle headed south through Barisha, Maven’s AI detected a vehicle that the U.S. military’s human eyes had missed. The ground commander then proceeded to call in the attack.

“At that moment, the helicopters arrived. Suddenly, we were hit. I didn’t know what was going on. I was just trying to escape death,” Barakat told NPR. His right arm was blown off, with his left hand partially disabled. His friends, Khaled Mustafa Qurmo and Khaled Abdel Majid Qurmo, were killed.

The U.S. military ultimately [rejected](https://www.npr.org/2023/09/24/1198908166/the-sunday-story-npr-challenges-u-s-denial-of-civilian-harm-in-raid-on-isis-lead) Barakat’s claim of harm. The results of a second Pentagon review, opened after an NPR investigation, were never released.

[Related Inside the Trump Administration’s War on the International Criminal Court](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/17/trump-icc-sanctions-war-crimes/)

A spate of articles have hailed this as the [year of AI warfare](https://theintercept.com/2026/09/28/ai-military-nuclear-war-doomsday/) — from [Ukrainian drones](https://theintercept.com/2026/08/26/ai-drone-warfare-russia-ukraine-openai-anthropic/) to Israel’s algorithmic decision support systems. A recent project that I worked on tracked how the rapid and potentially dangerous introduction of AI is [transforming every part of the “kill chain.”](https://ai-killchain.airwars.org/)

The AI-powered attack on Barakat may have occurred seven years ago, but new research has shown that many of these systems had been fielded years earlier than previously known, prompting questions about the extent of artificial intelligence’s role in historical attacks — and how it has already impacted civilian harm.

Children pass destroyed houses near the Syrian village of Barisha on Oct. 27, 2019, after an operation by the U.S. military targeting Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, the leader of the Islamic State group. Photo: Ghaith Alsayed/AP

## Maven’s Dawn

The role of Maven in the [2019 Baghdadi attack](https://theintercept.com/2019/11/10/baghdadi-death-war-on-terror/) was only revealed this year in journalist Katrina Manson’s book “Project Maven,” which charts the development of U.S. algorithmic warfare through the program of the same name.

Project Maven sought to create the algorithms and platforms to fuse real-time data from multiple feeds — among them drones, radar, satellites, and text — to conduct detect threats, run pattern-of-life analysis, and track targets, in the service of accelerating military targeting.

[Related Google DeepMind Engineer Resigns in Protest of Pentagon Contract](https://theintercept.com/2026/10/21/google-deepmind-resign-ai-military-gaza/)

The U.S. military initially tapped Google as a technology partner for Project Maven. But Google [pulled out in 2018](https://theintercept.com/2019/03/01/google-project-maven-contract/), following [protests](https://theintercept.com/2018/06/01/google-drone-ai-project-maven-contract-renew/) about its involvement in AI targeting, and [Palantir stepped in](https://theintercept.com/2019/03/09/anduril-industries-project-maven-palmer-luckey/).

Maven’s most revolutionary aspects were twofold: the creation of a “single visualization tool” — in this case, Palantir’s Maven Smart System — to [house](https://www.theregister.com/on-prem/2026/03/13/pentagon-praises-palantir-tech-for-battlefield-strike-speed/5224851) the feeds, fuse them and turbocharge decision-making, better known as “decision support systems.”

The second transformative aspect was the training of AI algorithms on vast amounts of images and full motion video generated from drone surveillance and other aerial and space-based sensors — a collaborative effort involving [multiple defense contractors](https://theintercept.com/2019/03/09/anduril-industries-project-maven-palmer-luckey/), initially led by the Pentagon. Maven algorithms would then be deployed into conflict theaters and applied to data streams to detect objects or targets, in technology known as “computer vision.”

Since their introduction to the Iraq and Syria conflicts in December 2017, as reported by Manson, just how many of the U.S. strikes undertaken were aided by Project Maven algorithms remains classified. But some analysis is possible.

December 2017 also saw the introduction of Maven AI to Somalia, at Baledogle Airfield where U.S. special forces were stationed, according to Manson’s reporting. At that point, the [U.S. had run a covert campaign](https://theintercept.com/2024/03/07/pentagon-somalia-africa-terrorism-failure/) of special force raids, kidnappings, and drone strikes in Somalia for over a decade, targeting insurgent groups opposed to its allies — most prominently al-Shabab.

> The initial aim wasn’t accuracy. Instead, the goal was to get analysts used to having their jobs made easier by the tireless, unblinking stare of computer vision.

Maven’s AI models were first trained on thousands of hours of drone footage from the country. Its integration lead, Colin Carroll, told Manson that Somalia was “more of a free-for-all” than other higher-profile American conflicts at the time, such as Iraq, Syria, and Afghanistan. Manson writes that “the operational risks of messing up weren’t as high,” and that Maven’s detection mistakes were “how crews got better.”

The initial aim wasn’t accuracy: Maven’s algorithms got its detections wrong more often than not, as Manson reported. Instead, the goal was to get [analysts](https://theintercept.com/2021/10/24/drone-war-books-neil-renic-wayne-phelps/) used to having their jobs made easier by the tireless, unblinking stare of computer vision. And it was a major step to the ultimate prize of getting the broader military hooked on AI — a goal that U.S. military planners appear to have met.

Earlier this year, the U.S. deputy secretary of defense wrote to Pentagon leaders to announce that Palantir’s Maven Smart System would be made a program of record, [locking in use of the technology](https://www.reuters.com/technology/pentagon-adopt-palantir-ai-as-core-us-military-system-memo-says-2026-03-20/) across the U.S. military.

The Pentagon remains tight-lipped about AI’s role in given strikes, save for occasional authorized leaks or [disclosures](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-02-26/us-says-it-used-ai-to-help-find-targets-it-hit-in-iraq-syria-and-yemen) to select journalists. Therefore establishing the role of AI in civilian harm in a large enough sample of cases to draw significant conclusions is nigh impossible.

But data from the civilian harm watchdog Airwars — which has [tracked alleged U.S. strikes in Somalia](https://airwars.org/conflicts/us-forces-in-somalia) since 2007 — gives some understanding of what happened after computer vision was integrated into U.S. targeting.

In the two years up to the introduction of Maven in December 2017, Airwars documented 64 strikes attributed to U.S. forces in Somalia. In the two years after, that number rose to 153.

[Related Secret Pentagon Investigation Found No One at Fault in Drone Strike That Killed Woman and 4-Year-Old](https://theintercept.com/2023/11/12/somalia-drone-strike-civilian-deaths/)

This unsurprisingly coincided with a spike in civilians being harmed. In the 64 strikes in 2016 and 2017, Airwars documented a minimum of 25 civilians killed and a further eight injured. In the two years after the introduction of Maven, the civilian kill count rose to a minimum of 79 — a more than threefold increase.

There were other factors that contributed toward these trends. Shortly before Maven was fielded in 2017, President Donald Trump designated part of the country as an “[area of active hostilities](https://foreignpolicy.com/2017/03/30/trump-expands-war-authorities-to-target-militants-in-somalia/).” Previously, any U.S. strike in Somalia required near certainty that the intended target was present and civilians would not be harmed, but these rules were loosened. The Trump administration also reordered the military structure, making it easier for strikes to be signed off lower down the chain of command. At the same time, private contractors came to be used more extensively.

But this dramatic increase in strikes is consistent with the [goals](https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/project-maven-ai-us-airstrike-iraq-anthropic-b2929138.html) of Project Maven — which include finding more targets, and accelerating the targeting cycle.

> There is no evidence that the introduction of AI reduced harm or made targeting more accurate.

At the very least, there is no evidence, as [advocates claim](https://geneva.usmission.gov/2019/03/26/u-s-statement-on-laws-potential-military-applications-of-advanced-technology/), that the introduction of AI reduced harm or made targeting more accurate. In the two years before Maven’s introduction to Somalia, civilians were reported killed or injured in roughly 1 in 7 alleged U.S. strikes. In the two years after, that rose to more than 1 in 5.

In striking similarity to Barakat’s case, less than a year after Maven’s deployment in Somalia, on August 2, 2018, U.S. Africa Command struck and [killed](https://airwars.org/incidents/ussom138-c-august-2-2018) four individuals it claimed were “terrorists” in a vehicle. Amnesty International [found](https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/afr52/9952/2019/en/) that three civilians had been killed, prompting the command to declassify its assessment in a disclosure to The Intercept — revealing the [military didn’t know the identities of those killed](https://theintercept.com/2019/07/10/pentagon-airstrikes-civilian-casualties-somalia/).

## “Critical Juncture”

This week could mark a decisive moment for the use of artificial intelligence in war. At the United Nations conference on Certain Conventional Weapons, nations will decide on adopting a mandate to begin negotiations on a new treaty to regulate [autonomous weapons](https://theintercept.com/2026/08/26/ai-drone-warfare-russia-ukraine-openai-anthropic/).

“We are at a critical juncture,” said Nicole van Rooijen, executive director of the group Stop Killer Robots, a campaign group. “The vast majority of states worldwide are in favor of a new legally binding instrument on autonomous weapons systems.”

“The first and important step in setting norms for the limits of AI-enabled, accelerated use of force is the mandate to negotiate legally binding rules for autonomous weapon systems,” said Elke Schwarz, a professor of political theory at Queen Mary University of London.

Target identification AI models, such as Maven, would not be covered by current negotiations since the U.N. [definition](https://www.stopkillerrobots.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/WEB-Policy-Brief_Autonomous-Weapons-Systems_Key-issues-and-path-to-a-treaty_Stop-Killer-Robots.pdf) of autonomous weapons demands that a single system both autonomously select *and* strike a target.

“There is a whole separate [UN] process for AI in the military domain,” van Rooijen said, “and [for that] we are nowhere near a treaty process.”

[Related The Pentagon Asked OpenAI for Artificial Intelligence Designed to Rarely Say No](https://theintercept.com/2026/09/08/pentagon-openai-military-contract/)

What played out in Somalia in the years after Maven’s introduction — a surge in the number of strikes and associated civilian harm — is similar to trends tracked in other recent military confrontations by actors known to use AI-powered systems.

The joint U.S.–Israeli attack on Iran ushered in a new era of [AI-powered warfare](https://theintercept.com/2026/03/11/podcast-trump-ai-world-wars/). In the initial 40-day assault, the U.S. and Israel declared they [struck](https://theintercept.com/2026/03/11/iran-school-missile-investigation/) more than 17,000 targets — a pace of warfare [unparalleled](https://airwars.org/record-pace-of-strikes-in-iran-bombing-campaign-analysis) in modern conflict. Airwars found that on every single day, Iranian civilians were reported killed or injured, in a total of 264 [tracked](https://airwars.org/conflicts/israeli-iranian-and-us-forces-2026) civilian harm incidents.

In Somalia, the current Trump administration has already launched nearly [four times](https://www.defensepriorities.org/explainers/exiting-somalias-war-end-us-military-operations/) the number of airstrikes than that of the Biden administration in its entire period in office, with reports of grave consequences for civilians. Last November, a U.S. airstrike reportedly killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children. No investigation appears to have been launched into the attack and, when asked by The Guardian, U.S. officials [declined](https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/jun/16/somalia-us-trump-war-alshabaab-islamists-drone-airstrikes-civilian-deaths-children) to provide its casualty assessment of the incident.

How machine-learning algorithms have contributed to targeting errors is compounded by misleading statements by militaries using AI.

One such case was U.S. Central Command’s response to a March 2026 [investigation](https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/middle-east/ai-airstrike-civilian-killed-us-centcom-iraq-anthropic-b2926712.html) by Airwars and The Independent into the first known victim of an airstrike in which the use of AI-assisted targeting was acknowledged. The military command claimed that it had “no way of knowing” whether the strike in Iraq had relied on machine-learning algorithms, despite its chief technology officer initially claiming that it had.

## Next Chapter in AI Warfare

Meanwhile, another, quieter development is underway that seems poised to further transform AI-powered warfare. Initiated by the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, the U.S. military is [planning](https://www.defenseone.com/technology/2025/05/ai-helping-pentagon-go-finding-targets-predicting-threats/405279/) to embrace more complex versions of already-fraught computer vision models.

The “first generation” of models applied AI object detection algorithms to images and video feeds. However, in the “next chapter,” the NGA and private contractors have been training models to spot anomalies, thus detecting not just known threats but also potential ones.

As the NGA director [explained](https://www.defenseone.com/technology/2025/05/ai-helping-pentagon-go-finding-targets-predicting-threats/405279/) last year, it could be an adversary truck that’s out of place, or a weapons manufacturing facility that has become very busy or fallen quiet.

“Anomaly detection,” as it is known, takes computer vision one step further, by deciphering objects or targets from imagery and then applying machine reasoning to a scene to determine whether changes indicate potential threatening activity.

But computer vision-based targeting models have been plagued by inaccuracy, and therefore risks of civilian harm.

When deployed in new terrain, and where uncertain environmental conditions hinder its abilities to recognize and flag objects, the first generation of Maven models exhibited a detection accuracy [below 30 percent](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-06-25/pentagon-sees-broader-role-for-ai-in-setting-military-targets?accessToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzb3VyY2UiOiJTdWJzY3JpYmVyR2lmdGVkQXJ0aWNsZSIsImlhdCI6MTc4MjQyODk2OCwiZXhwIjoxNzgzMDMzNzY4LCJhcnRpY2xlSWQiOiJUSDc3RVlUOTZPU0cwMCIsImJjb25uZWN0SWQiOiI3RUQyQkMyREM0OEQ0RTMyQjgzNzQ5MTVDRjJDMUZEMCJ9.30_hqeLGp4SXVvoIENQyy76t5Ac19_Bf6SLb65emFpo&leadSource=uverify%20walldrop), according to Manson’s book. At times it was less than 10 percent.

[Related Pete Hegseth’s Military of the Future: Defined by AI and an Utter Lack of Oversight](https://theintercept.com/2026/10/08/hegseth-military-ai-drones-autonomous-war/)

Treaty process aside, the distinction between autonomous weapons — narrowly defined — and AI-powered target identification may be one without a meaningful difference. In 2024, a Maven military exercise [aimed](https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/mar/26/ai-got-the-blame-for-the-iran-school-bombing-the-truth-is-far-more-worrying) at achieving 1,000 targeting decisions in an hour, which translates per operator as a decision to select or dismiss a target every 72 seconds.

When decision support systems serve targeting intelligence to military analysts at such intensity, the [human](https://theintercept.com/2021/10/24/drone-war-books-neil-renic-wayne-phelps/) in the loop becomes meaningless, argues Schwarz, the political theory professor.

“The use of AI target identification systems in recent conflicts in the Middle East has accelerated targeting to the point where no human decision-maker in the loop can make a truly meaningful decision, thereby becoming the proverbial cog-in-the-(killing)-machine,” she said.

“In creating an illusion of human judgment, AI-enabled targeting systems are perhaps an even more problematic technology than fully autonomous ones.”

In response to questions from Airwars and The Intercept, a Palantir spokesperson said Maven’s “superior technology is critical to both deterrence, the avoidance of wars, and the protection of civilians in the case of war.”

“Thanks to [Maven Smart System],” the spokesperson continued, “the U.S. military is now better able to protect the American people from those that seek to harm us, and is better prepared, if necessary, to win wars in a responsible, precise, and technologically-dominant manner.”
