items.articleBody:
## Improving on a timeless recipe

The bezier curve is a staple of CAD and computer graphics. Like Bic pens, the design is decades old and they're everywhere. You'll often find them as the default or only choice in various illustration and animation tools.

Conceived by [Paul de Casteljau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_de_Casteljau) in 1959, and refined by [Pierre Bézier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Bézier) in the 1960s at Renault, the enduring appeal of the bezier curve lies in its simplicity. While more sophisticated curves have been invented, and [new ones continue to be proposed](https://linebender.org/blog/hyperbezier/), these are limited to specific domains, like high-precision CAD or road design. In general use, the bezier stubbornly refuses to be dethroned, despite its shortcomings.

Hence bezier curves are a piece of legacy tech we appear to be stuck with. As a software engineer, my question then is: can we make beziers better without invalidating all the tech built on and with them?

The answer is yes.

[↗ wallup.net](https://wallup.net/renault-4cv-classic-cars-french-73/)

## Lerp-a-derp

Drawing a bezier curve is a surprisingly simple and linear process:

*Tip: All the diagrams in this post are fully interactive.*

Given a series of control points, we connect them with lines. We then run along those lines simultaneously, to produce new points, which can be connected again. This process is repeated until we are left with a single point, which lies on the curve.

This construction makes beziers far more regular than they might first appear.

The linear interpolations (aka *lerps* ) can be summarized into a single compact formula, e.g. for 4 control points $ \left(A, B, C, D\right) $:

$$ \gamma \left( t \right) = A \cdot \left(1 - t\right)^3 + B \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right)^2 t + C \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right) t^2 + D \cdot t^3 $$

The rule is simple: descending powers of $\left(1 - t\right)$, ascending powers of $t$, with coefficients taken from the n'th row of Pascal's triangle:

$$
\ {ccccccccccccc}
&&&&&& 1 \\
&&&&& 1 && 1 \\
&&&& 1 && 2 && 1 \\
&&& 1 && 3 && 3 && 1 \\
&& 1 && 4 && 6 && 4 && 1 \\
&1 && 5 && 10 && 10 && 5 && 1 \\
... &&&&&&... &&&&&&... \\
\ $$

For curves in 2D and 3D, the formula is applied to the individual X, Y or Z coordinates.

While beziers can be constructed for any number of control points, the common practice is to only use cubic beziers with 4 control points. This is because the curve is only guaranteed to cross through the first and last control point, which makes higher degree beziers more difficult to shape.

Larger curves are instead constructed by joining together multiple cubic bezier segments, with the tangents lined up to create a segmented curve that appears smooth:

This is the cubic bezier *spline*, as commonly understood. The precision "pen tool" in most drawing apps then consists of drawing and editing the control points, rather than drawing curves directly.

## A Lie Told Everywhere

Pen tools typically have a few different modes for the control points:

Intuitively these represent various degrees of smoothness. Symmetric tangents are offered as the smoothest option, with some qualities of smoothness being lost as you relax the constraints.

In reality this is **completely wrong**, and this is easy to demonstrate.

Bezier curves can be split exactly, by reading off the new control points from the interpolation diagram:

The left and right segments are 100% identical to the original curve, and always join up perfectly at the seam. Yet the tangents in the middle will be asymmetric except for one split near the middle. This can be confirmed using a *curvature comb* which represents the (inverse) radius of curvature at every point:

The curvature comb remains continuous, with no jumps.

This means that whether or not adjacent tangents are of equal length, i.e. symmetric, is completely irrelevant. Attempting to draw smooth and intuitive bezier curves this way is a fool's errand.

A simple way to improve this is to treat the tangents as relative rather than absolute. e.g. We can make them proportional to the distance between the start and end of each segment:

This spline is easier to edit, because as you move each curve point around, the adjacent segments naturally flex to get out of the way. There are far fewer cusps created this way. Editing the tangents remains the same.

However if we plot curvature again, we can tell this isn't a great solution:

Scaling tangents proportionally doesn't guarantee that curvature is preserved as you edit, nor does curvature remain continuous from one segment to the next.

This also shows that offering users a curvature comb visualization as a "helpful tool" is really quite *mean*: adjusting the curvature on one end will also affect the other side, requiring repeated adjustments back and forth until it's close enough.

## Handle Carefully

A much more effective strategy is to work with curvature directly.

While this is a difficult problem in general, it turns out there are some surprising relationships here, which we can observe directly:

Consider the curvature at the start of segment $A-B-C-D$. This is affected only by the positions of $A$, $B$ and $C$. Point $D$ can be moved freely if it's detached from $C$.

Furthermore, because the tangent $A-B$ is horizontal, only the vertical position of $C$ matters. This is a result of the underlying linear interpolations, which end up cancelling out a lot of terms in the formulas.

The curvature at $A$ is therefor only affected by the length of $A-B$, and the perpendicular distance from $C$ to $A-B$. The same applies to $D$ on the other side with $C-D$ and $B$.

This isn't very useful by itself though. When we move a curve point ($A$ or $D$), typically the adjacent control point ($B$ or $C$) is moved as well to preserve the tangent. And when we turn a symmetric or asymmetric tangent, the adjacent tangent in the next segment is turned by the same angle, altering the curvature on that side.

Still, this shows that preserving curvature is not by itself a crazy idea and can be done simply by scaling the tangents appropriately. The rules would be simple:

- When we move a curve point, we have to preserve the start and end curvature in the adjacent segments
- When we move a tangent, we have to preserve the curvature on the opposite end of the current segment, as well as on both sides of the adjacent segment

This ought to produce an editing experience where the curve actually respects your intent. Except not quite:

Moving curve points works great, but when turning a tangent, the length of that tangent is itself a poor representation of the user's intent. Small changes can cause huge shifts in curvature, which can cause the curve to jump around and explode unexpectedly as it tries to find a matching solution.

Hence it's better to work with curvature handles instead, where the length corresponds directly to curvature:

Unlike the curvature comb, the length of the handles is the non-inverted radius of curvature, which is the more natural choice.

These handles are very stable and can be converted just-in-time to classic bezier control points, without needing to round-trip back and forth between the two representations. Helpfully, this also avoids numerical drift.

## Goldilocks

To actually pull this off, we need to solve for the lengths $l_0$ and $l_1$ of the tangents, given the desired curvatures $k_0$ and $k_1$, the start/end points $A$ and $D$, and the unit-length tangents at the start/end.

Given a curve $\gamma\left(t\right)$, we can express the unit tangent vector $\ \left(t\right)$ as the normalized derivative:

$$ \ \left(t\right) = \ {\displaystyle |γ'\left(t\right)|} $$

This can be used to find the curvature vector $\ \left(t\right)$ via two vector cross products using the first and second derivative:

$$ \ \left(t\right) = \ \left(t\right) \times \ {|\gamma'\left(t\right)|^2} \times \ \left(t\right) $$

The cross products ensure that $\ \left(t\right)$ is perpendicular to $\ \left(t\right)$, i.e. they extract the normal vector component of the middle term. Now we can solve for $\ \left(0\right) = k_0$ and $\ \left(1\right) = k_1$.

After working through the math, we end up with a quadratic system of equations in $l_0$ and $l_1$:

$$
\ a_0 \cdot l_0^2 + b \cdot l_1 + c_0 = 0 \\[0.3em]
a_1 \cdot l_1^2 + b \cdot l_0 + c_1 = 0
\ $$

Where:

$$
\ {lcl}
a_0 & = & ±|k_0| \\[0.3em]
a_1 & = & ±|k_1| \\[0.3em]
b & = & 2 \cdot |\ (0) \times \ (1)| \\[0.3em]
c_0 & = & 6 \cdot |\ (0) \times (D - A)| \\[0.3em]
c_1 & = & 6 \cdot |\ (1) \times (A - D)| \\[0.3em]
\ $$

This captures a few things:

- The sign of the curvature $k_i$ defines whether the curve turns clockwise or counterclockwise. When moving curve points around, the curve may be forced to flip, hence the $±$ is necessary, and both signs can change independently.
- The coupling between $l_0$ and $l_1$ is influenced only by $b$. If $b = 0$, then the two equations are independent and the problem is trivial to solve. This corresponds to the situation where the two tangents are parallel.
- The constant term $c_i$ is influenced only by the perpendicular distance $D - A$ (or $A - D$) to the tangent $\ $. This matches the earlier finding that only perpendicular distance affects curvature.

Hence, the problem is reduced to finding the intersection of two double-parabolas, one horizontal and one vertical:

The two sides of each double-parabola represent bending clockwise or counterclockwise. We have to solve 4 times, one for each sign combination $\left(+,+\right)$, $\left(+,-\right)$, $\left(-,+\right)$, $\left(-,-\right)$.

To solve this system, we can rewrite either of the equations to isolate $l_1$ or $l_0$:

$$
l_1 = \ {\displaystyle b} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \ {\displaystyle b}
$$

Pick one, and square it to plug it into the other original equation as the $l_1^2$ or $l_0^2$ term. This produces a quartic equation in the other variable (resp. $l_0$ or $l_1$), which can be solved directly using the quartic formula.

We can then compute the other $l_i$, either:

$$
l_1 = \ {\displaystyle a_1}} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \ {\displaystyle a_0}}
$$

Not all solutions of the quartic will be actual solutions to the system however, because of the squaring. So we have to double check that the original equations hold before accepting a solution for $\left(l_0, l_1\right)$.

We also want to reject solutions where $l_0 < 0$ or $l_1 < 0$, because these represent situations where the tangents have been flipped by 180º.

In most cases, there will only be one valid solution, and this works pretty well:

For corner-type points, one or both $k_i$'s are infinite. This is straightforward to solve as the matching $l_i$ is zero and the other can be computed directly.

## Grouper and Snapper

Unfortunately if there are multiple solutions, these each represent a different curve:

Having the curve jump around as you edit it would be a very bad editing experience, but there is no obvious way to pick the right one.

One strategy would be to remember the previous $l_0$ and $l_1$ as you edit, and pick the solution that is closest to the previous curve. However this would introduce path-dependence into editing, where the order and direction that you moved points around in affects which curve you end up with. For a drawing tool, this is quite frustrating and undesirable.

Different solutions to the equation can also appear and vanish suddenly, so this wouldn't eliminate popping either, merely reduce it.

Ideally the resulting curvatures should always change smoothly themselves. This can be accomplished by designing an appropriate weighting heuristic for the solutions, and calculating their weighted average.

1) The forbidden regions:

When a solution approaches either $l_0 < 0$ or $l_1 < 0$, it's about to vanish, so its weight should go to zero there.

2) When two opposite-bending parabolas are about to become tangent, two solutions will move towards each other, before both vanishing at the same time:

These solutions are unstable and should be avoided. To detect this, I calculate the gradient vector of each equation.

$$
\ = \ 2 \cdot a_0 \cdot l_0 & b\ \\[0.3em]
\ = \ b & 2 \cdot a_1 \cdot l_1\ $$

The angle between them can be found via their dot product, after dividing by their respective lengths:

$$
\cos \theta = \ \cdot \ }{\displaystyle |\ ||\ |}
$$

A value close to $-1$ means two opposite-bending parabolas, while a value close to $1$ means two aligned parabolas. The latter is not as bad, as this implies many almost-equivalent solutions.

3) When the radius of curvature is very big compared to the bezier itself, one of the possible solutions is for the curve to cross through itself, forming a loop. This should be discouraged:

We can divide by the length of $|\ |$ i.e. $\ $, preferring solutions that have shorter tangents.

Putting it all together, the weighting heuristic I chose is:

$$
\left(\ \right) = \left(\ {\displaystyle |\ |^2}\right)^2
$$

- By applying $\arccos \left(-\cos \theta\right)$, we remap the dot-product range $(-1..1)$ to $(0..π)$ which effectively neutralizes the unstable solutions
- Large $|\ |$'s represent undesirable solutions, so should be strongly penalized and only chosen if they are the only option
- When the entire heuristic approaches $0$, the influence should vanish smoothly, hence the overall squaring

Using this as the weight, the resulting bezier curves always change smoothly, even when the start and end are moved around and through each other.

But when multiple solutions are averaged together, the resulting $(l_0, l_1)$ is not necessarily a solution to the original system. This means the resulting curvatures are not always exact, even when there is an exact solution nearby.

To mitigate this, we can add an additional resampling step, where we re-weigh the solutions according to the inverse distance^4 to the weighted average:

$$
\left(\ \right) = \ {|\ - \ |^4}
$$

This causes the solution to snap smoothly to exact solutions when available.

## Migratory Curves

What's especially nice about this approach is that it can largely be slotted into existing systems with little modification required.

The UI of adjusting and editing bezier handles can be kept, including the notion of the 4 point types. Just the meaning of the lengths of the tangents changes. Converting an asymmetric point to a symmetric point will actually equalize the curvature of the left and right side, which is what the user actually wants.

The internal representation can mostly remain the same type, i.e. a series of points, just those points represent curvature tangents, not bezier tangents. Though it's better to explicitly store the unit length tangents and curvatures directly, which is more numerically stable. For the demos here I made pairwise conversion functions between curvature handles ↔︎ points/tangents/curvatures ↔︎ bezier handles.

Splitting a curvature bezier is a lot simpler than splitting a classic bezier, because the start and end handles don't change at all, and the newly created handles are symmetric:

There is one remaining flaw though. When splitting a curve with an S-bend, the splits near the bend are not exact:

The heuristic picks the wrong curve on one or both sides. This can be fixed by remembering the specific orientation of the curvature, and only flipping the curvature sign when necessary. Though this does introduce some minimal path-dependence into editing.

So really you would need to expose this in the UI as an extra orientation toggle for ambiguous control points. It would also mean that the internal representation has to be in tangent + signed curvature form to be fully stable, not just curvature handles.

Near the S-bend, the radius of curvature—and thus the handle size—effectively becomes infinite, because $|k|$ becomes $0$. The bezier control points lie on a straight line, as perpendicular distance to the tangent is zero.

So even when handled exactly, this can still create impractically large curvature handles. Perhaps what's needed is a 5th "Inflection" point type, for points with exactly zero $|k|$, though such points tend to be very unstable, and sometimes no solution exists:

To migrate a classic bezier to a curvature bezier, you can measure the unit tangents and curvature at the start and end. In the vast majority of cases this will result in the exact same curve. If it doesn't, then you must split the original bezier to avoid the ambiguity.

For complex operations on bezier curves, e.g. boolean union or intersection, these still have to be done in bezier form. This implies some amount of round-tripping between the two representations, which would introduce numerical drift. However, only the newly created points need to be converted back, because the curvature and tangents elsewhere remain the same.

* * *

This post started from the observation that "symmetric" bezier tangents aren't actually symmetric as you'd expect. Hopefully you found the resulting exploration enlightening.

The practice of showing curvature combs to diagnose problems with splines is really backwards. If we can show a curvature comb, we can also compute an appropriate spline to match the desired curvature.

So beziers as they commonly exist are quite inadequate. We can retrofit a better system to edit them without breaking the expectations of a smooth editing experience, or introducing a new class of curves that behaves very differently.

*The code for the diagrams and implementation can be found on [GitLab](https://gitlab.com/unconed/bezbox/-/blob/master/src/graph/bez.ts?ref_type=heads#L61).*

APOD

Astronomy Picture of the Day

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

## A Medium-Sized Solar Flare

**Explanation:** What a [flare for the chromatic](https://idioms.thefreedictionary.com/flair+for+the+dramatic)! [Today’s image](http://galaxlux.com/Sun-%20Solar%20Limb%20Dynamics%2014%20May%202025.htm) captures a piece of the [Sun](https://science.nasa.gov/sun/)’s [chromosphere](https://scied.ucar.edu/learning-zone/sun-space-weather/chromosphere), the [layer of the Sun](https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/the-sun-spot/2023/09/26/layers-of-the-sun/)’s atmosphere above its surface where the temperature *rises*. Why would the Sun become hotter farther away from its [core](https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/sun-heat/en/)? This is potentially due to energy from the swirling [magnetic fields](https://solarscience.msfc.nasa.gov/the_key.shtml) extending up through the Sun’s atmosphere. Those same magnetic fields can [twist and snap](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/20310#media_group_320369), releasing light and energetic particles as a [solar flare](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oOXVZo7KikE). The [H-alpha filter](https://skyandtelescope.org/stargazing-and-observing/guide-to-observing-the-sun-in-h-alpha092321050923/) used for today’s image captures light from energized hydrogen atoms as they travel off the Sun’s surface during a flare on May 14, 2025. This flare was [classified](https://solar-center.stanford.edu/sid/activities/flare.html) as an M1 based on [GOES](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/goes/) [observations](https://www.spaceweatherlive.com/en/archive/2025/05/14/xray.html), meaning it was moderately bright in [X-rays](https://science.nasa.gov/ems/11_xrays/). M-class flares can cause [radio blackouts](https://www.spaceweather.gov/phenomena/solar-flares-radio-blackouts) at Earth’s poles and minor [radiation storms](https://www.spaceweather.gov/phenomena/solar-radiation-storm) that can harm astronauts. They aren’t even [the most powerful flares](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2018-september-2-a-powerful-solar-flare/)! NASA, [NOAA](https://www.noaa.gov/), and other agencies monitor the Sun to predict and identify such storms so we can protect humans on Earth and in space.

items.articleBody:
arXiv:2611.21682v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for knowledge-intensive and safety-critical applications in nuclear engineering. However, existing nuclear-domain benchmarks provide limited content coverage or focus primarily on answer accuracy without systematically evaluating the quality of the underlying reasoning. This study introduces NEBench R1, a reasoning-oriented benchmark comprising 7,546 unique multiple-choice questions extracted from U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) reactor operator licensing examinations covering 18 nuclear facilities. Each question is classified according to the NRC Knowledge and Abilities catalogs and accompanied by an official explanation serving as a reference for reasoning evaluation. Six LLMs were evaluated, with overall accuracy ranging from 34.0% to 73.9% across three distinct performance tiers. To assess reasoning quality, an LLM-based judge evaluated correctly answered responses using a multidimensional rubric. Although responses generally demonstrated strong problem comprehension, they scored lower in factual and procedural accuracy and distractor analysis, indicating that correct answers were not necessarily supported by technically sound justifications. Response clarity was also weakly indicative of technical quality. Furthermore, longer reasoning traces were associated with lower accuracy in both frontier reasoning models, suggesting that reasoning length may reflect question difficulty rather than improved problem-solving performance. Reasoning-token consumption may therefore provide an additional signal for identifying potentially unreliable responses. NEBench R1 establishes a benchmark for evaluating both answer accuracy and reasoning quality, providing a foundation for assessing the domain competence and reliability of LLMs in nuclear engineering.

items.articleBody:
A teacher who believes a student’s term paper may have been written by a large language model (LLM) can use a tool for detecting artificial intelligence-generated text to help confirm their suspicions. But the teacher may want to think twice before putting all their trust in the detector.

Researchers from MIT and Cornell University showed that such detection tools, which are AI models themselves, can be fooled by AI-generated text disguised to appear as if it were written by a human. Detectors can also fail to identify AI text due to natural shifts in writing habits over time or the emergence of new LLMs.

In a [new paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.25152), the researchers demonstrated how a special training technique makes an AI detector more accurate and resilient to deception, even as human and AI writing constantly changes.

They employed a method called test-time adaptation, which allows a deployed detection model to learn from new, unlabeled data by adjusting its inner workings on the fly. In this way, the model adapts to unseen inputs without being retrained from scratch.

In experiments, a commercial detector could only identify about 27 percent of AI-generated text that had been disguised, while the new approach achieved 93 percent accuracy.

This method could help educators, editors, publishers, and hiring managers flag LLM-generated writing that people try to pass off as human-written. It could also be used by cybersecurity experts to prevent email phishing scams or identify search engine optimization fraud.

“There are many high-stakes contexts where people really care about the identity of the author, from scientific publishing to short story competitions. We’ve shown that test-time adaptation allows your AI detector to be much more robust, even with continual adversarial behavior by AI users,” says study co-author Manish Raghavan, the Drew Houston (2005) Career Development Professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management, who also holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS).

He is joined on the paper by lead author Kevin Ren, graduate student at Cornell Tech, and senior author Nikhil Garg, an assistant professor at Cornell Tech. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.

**Duping the detectors**

The proliferation of LLMs that generate human-like text has led to a plethora of commercial AI-detection tools to help people identify whether a piece of writing was authored by a human.

But these detection tools can fail when the text they evaluate significantly differs from the text they were taught to identify. This is known as a distribution shift.

Detector developers typically train their models by gathering text from the internet that they know to be either AI- or human-generated. They train the model to tell the difference.

However, once the detector is released, people might change the way they write or the way they use AI to generate text.

For instance, a human in 2030 may write about different topics using new analogies that weren’t common for someone writing in 2010. A detector trained with 2010 data might be unfamiliar with this new writing style and incorrectly mark human-written text as AI-generated.

The release of a detection model also creates a cat-and-mouse game between its developers and users who want to bypass it. These individuals can run AI-generated text through an automated “humanizer” software tool that modifies it to appear human-written to the detector.

“After the company releases a model, a bunch of ‘humanizers’ pop up to try to beat it, so the company tries to incorporate this humanized text into their training so the detector can identify it, and so on. It’s like rinse-and-repeat. The cycle can go on forever,” says Ren.

The researchers explored whether test-time adaptation (TTA) can make an AI detector resilient to these distribution shifts.

**Adaptation in action**

In TTA, instead of freezing the model so it can’t change during deployment, researchers allow that model to adapt itself to incoming data after it has been released. For an AI text detector, these data are new pieces of text uploaded by users.

These data are unlabeled, so the detector developers don’t know which data were written by humans versus AI models. But these new data represent contemporary human and AI writing — exactly what the developers want the model to be able to predict.

With enough examples, the detector learns to identify patterns to determine which data are AI-generated and which are human-generated.

The researchers studied TTA by creating datasets to contain a certain amount of AI-generated and human-generated text, but they don’t provide those labels to the model. They also used LLMs to generate some examples that resemble text written by AI to specifically evade a detector.

Then they performed the TTA training process and tested the model on ground-truth data.

In experiments designed to mimic the natural shift in human language over time, a detector that used TTA was 85 percent accurate, while traditional methods only achieved 73 percent accuracy.

And when it came to writing designed to thwart detection tools, existing methods could only identify about 27 percent, while TTA enabled the model to catch more than 93 percent of disguised text.

“TTA has the potential to really help deployed AI-detection models in terms of being able to proactively address this iterative ‘gaming’ behavior by adversarial AI users,” Ren says.

Adapting to shifts in human writing behavior is a more difficult TTA problem, since the shifts are slower and occur in more subtle ways, he adds.

The researchers caution that TTA may not always be an effective solution as future LLMs produce more natural-sounding language and it becomes harder to find verifiable human text to use for training.

“It isn’t entirely clear if this will be a solvable problem,” Raghavan says. “There are some big, open questions about how you should think about science, writing, and art in a world where it is infeasible to tell the difference between human-generated content and AI content.”

In the future, the researchers want to explore similar strategic domains where TTA could be useful and build better benchmarking tools to help engineers improve these AI detection models in a dynamic fashion.

This project used API credits provided by Pangram to use their AI text detectors.

items.articleBody:
When Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election, I was in the last place I wanted to be: Washington, DC. Where would I go? I wanted nothing to do with his administration’s empty grandeur. I spent the day at Maya Lin’s Vietnam War Memorial, a dark wound in the earth. In this much more hopeful moment post-midterms, Ed Simon asks a related question: How should memorials remember the MAGA era? He points to historical anti-fascist examples in Germany — and also suggests the bulldozing of Trump’s ballroom to rubble as its own kind of monument.

Satire’s not a bad strategy to record this era, either. Also today, Greg Werkheiser pens an obituary for the National Historic Preservation Act. The act’s next of kin, the National Register of Historic Places, he writes, “is said to be concerned about its own health.”

Finally, don’t miss the newest installation of Jennifer Samet’s “Beer With a Painter” column. She interviews Ivorian painter Ouattara Watts, who works only at night, when the veil between this world and the next is thinnest. Plus, The Met and the Shanghai Museum are teaming up, just weeks after MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Museum joined forces. They say art imitates life; I just didn’t know that meant we were getting museum oligopolies.

*—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor*

[How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?](https://hyperallergic.com/how-should-we-memorialize-the-trump-era/)

items.articleBody:
Is an image of Margaret Qualley, Madelyn Cline and Sabrina Carpenter a real ad from Palantir? No, that's not true: The photo is from the set of Carpenter's "House Tour" music video and edited to add the Palantir branding. The account that posted the image is a satire account.

The claim appeared in [a post](https://x.com/palantirletter/status/2119129296279101696) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](http://web.archive.org/web/20261112030717/https://x.com/PalantirLetter/status/2119129296279101696) ) by the @PalantirLetter account on X on Nov. 7, 2026. It read:

> Margaret Qualley, Madelyn Cline, and Sabrina Carpenter for Palantir

This is what the post looked like on X at the time of writing:

*(Image source: post by @PalantirLetter on X.)*

The PalantirLetter account on X is a parody account. The bio reads, "Palantir Newsletter, you've been on it longer than you think. Nobody featured endorses Palantir the corporation. All posts are strictly satire." Palantir is a supplier of AI-powered data analytics tools.

This is a screenshot of the account on X at the time of writing:

*(Image source: @PalantirLetter on X.)*

The image was originally posted on Cline's Instagram account [@madelyncline](https://www.instagram.com/p/DZfgdIOFhAJ/?img_index=12) on June 12, 2026. It is a still shot from the set of Carpenter's music video "House Tour." Entertainment publication [Variety](https://variety.com/2026/music/news/sabrina-carpenter-margaret-qualley-steal-a-grammy-house-tour-video-1236709136/) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20260511032304/https://variety.com/2026/music/news/sabrina-carpenter-margaret-qualley-steal-a-grammy-house-tour-video-1236709136/) ) wrote about the music video, noting Qualley and Cline joined Carpenter on set.

This is what the image looked like on Cline's Instagram account at the time of writing:

*(Image source: post by @madelyncline on Instagram.)*

Had Carpenter, Qualley and Cline appeared in a Palantir ad, it would likely have been major news. Lead Stories searched [Google News](https://www.google.com/search?sca_esv=c7d303c55049bf1d&sxsrf=AKL5yDjosNOSqyuT9lYHpof-nHBcEyFg5A:1794960281155&q=Margaret+Qualley,+Madelyn+Cline+and+Sabrina+Carpenter+Palantir+ad&tbm=nws&source=lnms&fbs=ACAhTvwdifjn2dKXmjtOfBxVFl_koHVe5RLSnJlTH2QYaq_YVdLmrLcUHX_SwxOCJnubtIIHVRoe-tT9uyqq1HrjHtbccZFzexuKafeIafLOkJG1yAcEZnJFHMjy91U2XeKflcnzzV_1V90wmFB5vcAGeswx_7FtchzYLt6rfCTeBTMfgEWjUBsj6LuW804lc8WY0UNBf2ABpBBO4l9m44HgmQXZ2-Ot3w&sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwicssaPnJCYAxWmLkQIHfXRLa4Q0pQJegQIGhAB&biw=1710&bih=895&dpr=2) and [Yahoo News](https://search.yahoo.com/news/search;_ylt=A2RQLuhI7PxqwgIAse5XNyoA;_ylu=Y29sbwN1cy13ZXN0LTIEcG9zAzIEdnRpZAMEc2VjA3BpdnM-?p=Margaret+Qualley%2C+Madelyn+Cline+and+Sabrina+Carpenter+Palantir+ad&fr2=piv-web&fr=yfp-t) using the search terms "Margaret Qualley, Madelyn Cline and Sabrina Carpenter Palantir ad" and did not find any matching news reports from established news outlets.

items.articleBody:
Many will recall **Erland Cooper**as the composer who buried the only copy of**[Carve the Runes Then Be Content With Silence](https://acloserlisten.com/2024/09/17/erland-cooper-carve-the-runes-then-be-content-with-silence)** in the ground, then challenged fans to find it, dig it up and return it. *Dawn Chorus* is a different beast, still in love with the great outdoors but noticeably above ground. Recorded with the BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra featuring violinist Freya Goldmark, the set unfolds in four sumptuous suites, ending in notes as triumphant as the dawn.

When considering instrumental music, one rarely discusses earworms, although they do exist: the prominent attack of Beethoven’s Fifth, the lilting melody of “Für Elise,” and of course, “The Wedding March.” Cooper may have found his own in the six-note motif of “Paradisaea.” The composition rises from a series of quiet stringed passages, each falling into silence before rising again, giving way to the secondary and then the central theme. The composition imitates the slow blossoming of dawn, light peeking shyly over the horizon before announcing itself in full. A tender passage in the midst of the first movement indicates the fragility of the day before it has been established. Once that motif breaks through, so does the sun, and no amount of silence, no sonic shift can contain it.

Freya rises to a frenzy in the second movement, then relents, like a murmuration forming and dissipating. The third refreshes the motif, presenting it again in a round, by which point it has become lodged in the listener’s head. Drum rolls bring the piece to a rousing finale, waking the final residents of forest and field. “Erithacus rubecula” (“European Robin”) starts in far gentler fashion, with solo, exploratory notes, the single bird joined by the flock in the Allegretto. The dominant themes are wider, more expansive, like the light splayed across the countryside. The violin soars toward the heavens, outpacing the flock, unable to contain its excitement. The vast center of the Allegretto conjures images of prairies, unspoiled hopes and the splendour of a new day, while the third movement returns to the robin, undergirded by a gentle hum reflecting the warmth of the rising rays.

“Fratercula arctica” (“Atlantic Puffin”) is a surprisingly romantic composition. A series of lilting melodies leads to a swirl of orchestral activity, like a camera being drawn back to reveal an entire population. The second movement is calmer and more intimate, with hints of harp. Darker brass chords swoop in, revealing an unprecedented tension resolved by the early minutes of the Finale. This third movement is the album’s finest, earning its swoops of joy. The ending is so triumphant and seemingly definitive that on first play, one receives it as the end of the album and rises for an exuberant Bravo! ~ only to realize that there’s still one suite to come.

“Unfolding Landscapes” is a combination of encore, outlier and denouement. The shortest suite (unfolding in only two movements) and the only one to eschew Latin titles, the composition is also distinguished by the rhapsodic piano of “Pt. 1,” which leads to full orchestral accompaniment in “Pt. 2.” A quickening of pace leads to friendly staccato strings, which pause for a few regal seconds before racing to *Dawn Chorus’* s second, even grander finale. Drums join the fray, at first restrained and finally booming, a hummingbird tempo toppling into a bevy of brass. Two seconds of silence are followed by a 20-second cinematic peak. And now the album is *really* over, the sun erupting through the clouds, the earth rejoicing and every living creature giving praise. **(Richard Allen)**

items.articleBody:
This privately funded, not-for-profit museum lets visitors witness the greatness and trials of the teams that made up the "Original Eight" of the Negro Leagues.

In a self guided tour explore the informative and interactive exhibits featuring the photos, artifacts and films that tell the stories of these baseball players and all the people that made these teams possible.

Notable highlights include:

The Exhibition Gallery Film entitled "They Were All Stars" with narration by the acclaimed James Earl Jones. This film is a museum exclusive.

A timeline of baseball and African American history along with one-of-a-kind photographs, artifacts and stories to better envision the legacies told!

The Field of Legends that allows you to step into history with a stunning recreation of a baseball diamond, featuring bronze statues of all the greatest League players in their starring positions.

items.articleBody: Intracranial aneurysm (IA) is a focal dilation of the cerebral artery wall whose rupture causes aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage with approximately 40% case fatality. No intervention exists at the initiation stage because clinical imaging cannot resolve the cellular events that precede overt morphological change. We propose that pericyte dysfunction at the cerebral microcirculation barrier is the upstream event linking abnormal hemodynamics to IA initiation. Under physiological laminar shear, Piezo1–Notch mechanosensing and basal TGFβ–ALK5 signaling maintain the pericyte-supported microcirculation barrier; under disturbed flow, pericytes undergo HK2-driven glycolytic reprogramming, pro-inflammatory conversion, and contractile gain, causing focal barrier leakage. Leaked inflammatory mediators and plasma macromolecules are conveyed by cerebrospinal-fluid convection through the perivascular space to the adventitia of adjacent circle-of-Willis arteries, driving smooth muscle cell (SMC) shift toward a dedifferentiated, synthetic phenotype, expansion of POSTN+ perivascular fibroblasts, matrix degradation, internal elastic lamina destruction, and decompensated fibrosis culminating in saccular aneurysm. This cascade repositions aneurysm-wall fibrosis as an early event, opening a preventive window. We outline stage-matched interventions (HK2 metabolic axis, TGFβ/POSTN fibrosis axis, senolysis) and decisive experiments, including in vivo two-photon tracing of microcirculation-to-large-artery signaling through the perivascular space, with the evidence for each link explicitly graded.

items.articleBody: Transcription and neuronal activity in the central nervous system generate abundant DNA damage, particularly DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), rendering neural cells - and cerebellar neurons especially - vulnerable to genome instability. Tyrosyl-DNA phosphodiesterase 2 (TDP2, also known as TTRAP) resolves topoisomerase-2-linked DSBs, and biallelic TDP2 mutations cause spinocerebellar ataxia autosomal recessive 23 (SCAR23), yet how DNA repair shapes human cerebellar development is unknown. Here we model SCAR23 in cerebellar organoids derived from patient induced pluripotent stem cells carrying TDP2 c.650del and from prime-edited isogenic TDP2 c.400C>T lines. TDP2 inactivation caused organoid hypoplasia during FGF8b-dependent cerebellar specification, which was reversed by TDP2 complementation. Single-nucleus transcriptomics across three developmental stages revealed early dysregulation of ribosome biogenesis, attenuated CREB1 regulon activity and a subsequent failure of Purkinje cell maturation. TDP2 inactivation upregulated PKIB, a cerebellum-enriched inhibitor of protein kinase A, lowering PKA and CREB phosphorylation. Whole-genome sequencing showed excess de novo deletions in mutant organoids, enriched at candidate cis-regulatory elements of neurodevelopmental genes. Pharmacological activation of the cAMP-PKA cascade restored CREB phosphorylation, reduced DNA damage and rescued organoid growth. These findings link developmental signalling to genome maintenance in the human cerebellum and identify the cAMP-PKA-CREB axis as a candidate therapeutic target in DNA-repair-deficient cerebellar disease.

items.articleBody:
The grounding of thousands of flights on Nov. 13 set off a round of partisan finger-pointing over who’s to blame for the state of the nation’s aging air traffic control system.

In social media posts over the weekend, President Donald Trump blamed the Biden administration for “making an old and broken system worse.” But as we’ve written [before](https://www.factcheck.org/2025/12/sorting-out-competing-claims-on-air-traffic-control/), the Federal Aviation Administration’s struggles to modernize the air traffic control system go back decades and span administrations of both political parties.

Democrats in Congress, meanwhile, have responded to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s calls for additional funding to modernize the air traffic control system by questioning why his department has spent only part of a $12.5 billion appropriation it received in 2025.

That funding lasts through the 2029 fiscal year, and Duffy has [said](https://www.nbcnews.com/meet-the-press/transcripts/meet-press-november-15-2026-rcna609426) the FAA will spend it all by then, though the agency has spent that money at a slower pace than it initially [projected](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/meetings/faas-plan-for-atc-modernization-evaluating-progress-ensuring-accountability-and-results/).

Duffy and other officials [have](https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/must-read-secretary-sean-p-duffy-op-ed-one-big-beautiful-bill-down-payment-brand-new) also been [clear](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/meetings/35474D94-0534-4F48-BA37-193607922957/TESTIMONY-FAA%20Administrator%20Bedford%20-%20SENATE.pdf) that they consider the $12.5 billion a “down payment” and that it will take additional funding to fully modernize the system. We’ll explain more about this funding and how it’s being used.

The Department of Transportation has [said](https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/icymi-us-transportation-secretary-sean-p-duffy-provides-update-restoration-airspace) the ground stop was caused by a technical issue with a new router installed by a contractor at a communications site, as part of the FAA’s efforts to replace old copper wiring with fiber-optic cable.

A former FAA official and outside experts [told](https://www.washingtonpost.com/transportation/2026/11/17/duffy-wants-50-billion-avert-another-ground-stop-experts-say-money-isnt-issue/) the Washington Post this week that a lack of funding was not the immediate cause of the failure, noting that efforts to overhaul the system have seen decades of delay and that upgrading older systems requires careful planning and redundancies.

“Nobody campaigns on the thrill of replacing old copper lines or painting rusting communications towers, so basic upkeep gets kicked down the road year after year,” [Lance Sherry](https://www.gmu.edu/profiles/lsherry), director of the Center for Air Transportation Systems Research at George Mason University, told us in an email. “It is the exact same logic as ignoring a check-engine light until the car breaks down on the highway.”

## Not Just a Biden Administration Issue

As we’ve explained [before](https://www.factcheck.org/2025/12/sorting-out-competing-claims-on-air-traffic-control/), efforts to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system go back to at least the 1980s, when the federal government contracted with IBM to lead implementation of what it called the Advanced Automation System. The FAA [scrapped](https://www.gao.gov/assets/t-rced/aimd-98-85.pdf) or scaled back much of the project in 1994 [after](https://www.gao.gov/assets/t-rced-94-188.pdf) years of delays and cost overruns, according to reports from the General Accounting Office, a nonpartisan congressional watchdog now called the Government Accountability Office.

In 2003, the FAA launched its Next Generation Air Transportation System, or [NextGen](https://www.faa.gov/nextgen), project, which aimed to modernize the country’s air traffic control system and other infrastructure by 2025. Despite putting $15 billion into the project, the FAA had achieved only about 16% of NextGen’s expected benefits by the end of 2024, according to a [report](https://www.oig.dot.gov/sites/default/files/library-items/NextGen%20Capstone%20Memo_9-29-25.pdf) from the Department of Transportation’s inspector general last year.

“Lengthy delays and cost growth have been a recurring feature of FAA’s modernization efforts through the course of NextGen’s over 20-year lifespan,” the report stated.

“So the FAA has a long history of problems that extended from the George W. Bush administration, through Obama, Trump I, and Biden,” [John Strong](https://mason.wm.edu/faculty/directory/strong-j.php), a professor and aviation-safety expert at the College of William & Mary, [told us](https://www.factcheck.org/2025/12/sorting-out-competing-claims-on-air-traffic-control/) last year.

Planes sit on the taxiway at San Diego International Airport after the FAA issued an emergency nationwide ground stoppage on Nov. 13. Photo by Luke Johnson / The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images.

Trump, in a pair of social media posts on Nov. 15, nonetheless placed the blame largely on his immediate predecessor.

“The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster,” he said in one Truth Social [post](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117620643696909295). “Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began.”

In another [post](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117620719333478761), he called on Congress to approve “desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control” and said the “Biden Administration set it back years!”

“Not sure I’d characterize it that way,” Strong told us in an email this week when we asked him about Trump’s posts.

“The system was under some strain prior to Covid, but … mostly operating OK,” Strong explained. “The biggest issue during the 2020-2022 period was the shutdown of the FAA Academy for 4 months in 2020, then reduced operations for nine months or more. The gap in training controllers, plus the fact that many controllers retired during Covid, contributed to the shortage of controllers that was real evident in the last years of the Biden period.”

Under Biden, the 2021 [Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/house-bill/3684/text) allocated $5 billion for air traffic control improvements, including replacing or upgrading towers, updating power and communications systems, and other infrastructure improvements, as well as hiring more air traffic controllers.

Strong told us last year that “the failure of [air traffic control] modernization predates the Biden administration,” but the funding under Biden “was mostly carrying on with plans that were inadequate in both scope and funding.” Most of it targeted “immediate problems” like staffing shortages and equipment breakdowns, he said.

Pete Buttigieg, who served as Biden’s transportation secretary, pushed back on the claims from Trump, who told reporters on Nov. 16 that “Buttigieg ruined the system.”

“As secretary, I made sure to leave air travel in better condition than when we arrived,” Buttigieg [said](https://x.com/PeteButtigieg/status/2122401936720695318) in an X post, pointing to efforts to hire more air traffic controllers and modernize communications infrastructure that predated Trump’s second term. “I am glad the Trump administration has continued that work, but they have so far failed to explain why their execution of it triggered the worst FAA communications breakdown this century.”

## FAA Funding

In the wake of last week’s ground stop, Duffy called on Congress to approve $50 billion in new funding for air travel infrastructure, including additional funds for air traffic control system upgrades.

The proposal has faced skepticism from lawmakers in both parties, with many noting that the Department of Transportation has spent less than half of the $12.5 billion it received for air traffic improvements in the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act that was championed by Trump.

“Trump is now asking for $50 billion, despite sitting on most of the $12.5 billion that Congress gave him last year,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer [said](https://www.c-span.org/clip/us-senate/schumer-says-faa-ground-stop-wouldnt-have-happened-if-trump-focused-more-on-air-travel-issues-instead-of-vanity-projects/5210908) in a Nov. 16 floor speech, adding that lawmakers “want to give them all the money they need — but they gotta use it and know how to implement it, and they don’t. Mr. President Trump, what happened to the $12.5 billion we gave you?”

Some Republicans have also questioned the administration’s latest funding request and noted the availability of much of the OBBBA funding, Politico [reported](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/16/trump-administration-air-traffic-demand-senate-01168724).

Whether Congress should approve more money is a policy debate, and we take no position on that. But here’s the context behind the $12.5 billion figure lawmakers are bringing up.

In May 2025, the Trump administration [announced](https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/us-transportation-secretary-sean-p-duffy-unveils-plan-build-brand-new-state-art-air) plans to build what it called a “brand-new state-of-the-art air traffic control system” by the end of 2028, [including](https://www.transportation.gov/sites/dot.gov/files/2025-12/Brand%20News%20Air%20Traffic%20Control%20System%20Fact%20Sheet.pdf) replacing outdated equipment and modernizing radar and communications networks. As we’ve [reported](https://www.factcheck.org/2025/12/sorting-out-competing-claims-on-air-traffic-control/), the project is an extension, and in some cases acceleration, of the NextGen initiative.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act — which Trump signed in July 2025 — provided $12.5 billion toward those efforts. Duffy was [clear](https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/must-read-secretary-sean-p-duffy-op-ed-one-big-beautiful-bill-down-payment-brand-new) at the time that he considered the money a “down payment” on what was expected to be a [$31.5 billion project,](https://www.rev.com/transcripts/ups-plane-crash-update) a point FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford [echoed](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/meetings/35474D94-0534-4F48-BA37-193607922957/TESTIMONY-FAA%20Administrator%20Bedford%20-%20SENATE.pdf) in December when speaking to a Senate subcommittee.

Of that $12.5 billion, $9 billion [was](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-26-107992/index.html?_gl=1*shxrvu*_ga*MjAxNTM2MjQ2Ny4xNzg2MTI4MTA0*_ga_V393SNS3SR*czE3OTQ4NDMyMzckbzkkZzAkdDE3OTQ4NDMyMzckajYwJGwwJGgw#_ftn24) specifically designated for modernizing telecommunications, radar and other air traffic control systems, with the remainder set aside for construction and consolidation of air traffic facilities. The law made the money [available](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-26-107992/index.html?_gl=1*shxrvu*_ga*MjAxNTM2MjQ2Ny4xNzg2MTI4MTA0*_ga_V393SNS3SR*czE3OTQ4NDMyMzckbzkkZzAkdDE3OTQ4NDMyMzckajYwJGwwJGgw#_ftn24) through Sept. 30, 2029.

Bedford [told](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/meetings/faas-plan-for-atc-modernization-evaluating-progress-ensuring-accountability-and-results/) lawmakers in December 2025 that he expected around $6 billion to $6.5 billion of the $12.5 billion would be [obligated](https://www.cbo.gov/publication/57660) — that is, legally committed to specific uses, such as a contract to purchase equipment — “by the end of the year.” (We asked the FAA whether Bedford meant the 2025 calendar year or the 2026 fiscal year, which ended Sept. 30, and haven’t heard back.) The DOT told us this week that more than $4 billion has been obligated so far, but all the money is “accounted for” in the sense that the department has a plan for how to spend it.

Specifically, out of the $12.5 billion, a DOT spokesperson told us the department has obligated 48% of the $4.8 billion appropriated for telecommunications upgrades (including the replacement of copper wire with newer technologies, which the department says is 70% complete). Meanwhile, 34% of the $3.5 billion appropriation for radars and other surveillance systems has been obligated, with that number expected to rise as more radar production comes online as soon as next month. The department said it has also obligated 63% of the $800 million it received for “foundational upgrades,” such as replacing old floppy disks and making aviation-safety improvements in Alaska.

The spokesperson said most of the final $3.4 billion, which is for facility construction and consolidation, won’t be spent until 2027 or 2028 because it’s less of a priority. Just 6% of that funding has been obligated so far.

“I think it took longer than many of us thought to select a prime contractor for the project, and to develop priorities,” Strong, the aviation-safety expert at William & Mary, told us. “But for many projects like this, early stage is [a] lower share, then [there is a] ramp up in the middle period as initiatives are rolled out systemwide. Overall, a bit slow, but not unprecedented.”

That’s not to say there haven’t been issues with the implementation. The Government Accountability Office released a report in September [criticizing](https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-26-107992.pdf#page=27) aspects of how the FAA has managed the rollout, saying it hadn’t developed an integrated master schedule or comprehensive cost estimate.

Hours before the ground stop, Duffy had [asked](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/white-house-urges-congress-provide-301-billion-aviation-reform-2026-11-13/) lawmakers to approve an additional $30 billion in funding for airport and air traffic control infrastructure. Asked for a breakdown of that funding, a Department of Transportation spokesperson referred us to a [fact sheet](https://www.transportation.gov/sites/dot.gov/files/2026-09/Modern%20Skies%20Act%20fact%20sheet.pdf) for the [Modern Skies Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/5572?hl=modern+skies+sky&s=2&r=2), a bill

On Nov. 13, after the nationwide ground stop, Duffy [upped](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-press-briefing-markwayne-mullin-sean-duffy-faa-ground-stop-november-13-2026/) his request to $50.1 billion. According to a Nov. 17 [letter](https://www.transportation.gov/sites/dot.gov/files/2026-11/Joint%20Letter%20Regarding%20Additional%20ATC%20Funding.pdf) from Duffy to leaders of the House and Senate appropriations committees, that includes $10.1 billion for “air traffic control modernization” including telecommunications and digital technology upgrades; $10 billion in discretionary grants for airport infrastructure improvements; $10 billion to “replace, modernize or fully reconstruct aging terminals at high-impact transitional hub airports”; $10 billion to build five consolidated air route traffic control centers to replace [nearly two dozen aging facilities](https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/trump-administration-calls-congress-fully-fund-air-traffic-control-modernization-501); and $10 billion to build, replace or improve up to 140 air traffic control towers.

Trump’s recent [budget](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BUDGET-2026-BUD/pdf/BUDGET-2026-BUD.pdf) [proposals](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/budget_fy2027.pdf) have asked for $4 billion for FAA facilities and systems upgrades, well short of what his administration is now requesting from Congress.

items.articleBody: ContextThe cerebral substrates of fatigue in patients with Multiple Sclerosis (pwMS) remain incompletely understood. This study aims at exploring the functional brain substrates of fatigue in pwMS with a recent disease history.MethodsSixteen pwMS (disease history < 5 years) and 17 matched Healthy Controls (HC) performed a N-Back task with three difficulty levels during functional MRI (fMRI) acquisitions following high vs. low cognitive fatigue induction. Measures of subjective trait and state fatigue were also recorded. Behavioral performance at the N-Back task and evolution of subjective fatigue states were analyzed by means of Bayesian repeated measures analyses of variance. fMRI data were analyzed to determine between-group differences (1) in task-related brain activity, independently of trait fatigue score; (2) in the association between trait fatigue and brain activity.ResultsEvidence toward a similar trajectory in the two groups was observed for subjective and task-related measures of fatigue following fatigue induction. No between-group difference was observed in brain activity unrelated to fatigue score. However, negative associations between trait fatigue score and brain activity were observed in pwMS, while the associations are positive in HC. Specifically, opposite associations (positive in HC and negative in pwMS) were observed in regions belonging to the Striato-Thalamo-Cortical (STC) network and the fronto-parietal cortex.ConclusionSlightly different patterns of brain activity related to fatigue were observed in pwMS and HC in the STC circuitry, despite similar behavioral performance and subjective fatigue level. This is consistent with the implication of the STC loops in fatigue pathophysiology, occurring from the early stages of the disease.

items.articleBody:
MIT students are going to office hours less often. They’re spending less time working through problem sets, and with one another. Those were among the findings of MIT’s recent report on [artificial intelligence and education](https://aiandeducation.mit.edu/report/), and they are one reason a growing number of MIT faculty are concerned about how generative AI is both changing how people work and affecting how they think, learn, and relate to one another.

For the [MIT Human Insight Collaborative](https://mithic.mit.edu) (MITHIC), those questions have become a central focus, and MITHIC is working with collaborators across the Institute, including the[Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing](https://computing.mit.edu/cross-cutting/social-and-ethical-responsibilities-of-computing/) (SERC), to help MIT address them.

Launched in 2024 as a strategic initiative, MITHIC brings together scholars, artists, educators, and researchers to explore the human dimensions of the defining challenges of our time. Since its launch, MITHIC has supported [67 projects across 31 MIT units](https://mithic.mit.edu/impact/), offering a total of $5.5 million in funding.

Roughly a third of those projects are focused on AI, society, and humanity — a topic that MITHIC faculty co-lead [Heather Paxson](https://anthropology.mit.edu/people/faculty/heather-paxson) says has become an increasingly important part of the initiative.

“When we refer to AI and society, we’re not only speaking about individual ethical decision-making or how to retrain workers. We’re looking at how AI is reshaping sociality, how we [relate](https://news.mit.edu/2026/when-we-talk-to-machines-sherry-turkle-book-0929) to one another,” says Paxson, a professor of anthropology and the associate dean of the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS).

**Eroding “creative friction”**

Building upon this focus, an [AI and Society Forum](https://news.mit.edu/2026/exploring-societal-impacts-of-ai-0623) took place on campus earlier this year. Co-organized by MITHIC, SHASS, SERC, and the[MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium](https://genai.mit.edu/) (MGAIC), the event featured presentations and panels concentrating on jobs, democracy, and AI.

On campus, the report on AI and education warned that AI is eroding the “creative friction” that has long defined an MIT education: students debating ideas and challenging one another, their professors, and their teaching assistants, in class and out of it.

MITHIC faculty co-lead [Seth Mnookin](https://cmsw.mit.edu/profile/seth-mnookin/), a science writing professor and head of Comparative Media Studies Program/Writing (CMS/W), said, “The report wasn’t saying that AI is here and we all need to adapt. It was saying that we need to be asking more fundamental questions.”

“When the United States entered World War II in 1941, the Institute’s newly minted scientists and engineers helped shape that era through science and technology,” Mnookin said. “We’re at a similarly consequential moment with AI. The difference is that this time, the questions that matter most can’t be answered by technologists alone. That’s where the humanities, arts, and social sciences come in.”

**Crossing disciplines in the pursuit of answers**

MITHIC is supporting a range of interdisciplinary projects through its [SHASS+ Connectivity Fund](https://mithic.mit.edu/shass-connectivity-fund/), in which a SHASS scholar partners with a researcher in another part of MIT.

In the context of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, political science professors [Adam Berinsky](https://polisci.mit.edu/people/adam-berinsky) and [Charles Stewart III](https://polisci.mit.edu/people/charles-stewart-iii) and MIT Sloan School of Management Assistant Professor [Chara Podimata](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/faculty/directory/chara-podimata) are studying how large language models (LLMs) have become intermediaries of democratic knowledge.

The ongoing project, which has demonstrated how voters in Alaska’s midterms who conducted their pre-election research using Anthropic’s AI model, Claude, may have received incomplete information about candidates and their views, was recently [featured in The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/10/business/media/ai-chatbots-election-misinformation.html?unlocked_article_code=1.IVE.8Kr5.eEpKyyfrOLzA&smid=url-share).

“AI is becoming part of the way people encounter and make sense of political information, and yet we know relatively little about what that information environment actually looks like, how it differs for different user demographics, political identities, and geographies,” Podimata told the *Times*.

In another project, CMS/W Professor [Eric Klopfer](https://cmsw.mit.edu/profile/eric-klopfer/) and brain and cognitive sciences Professor [Pawan Sinha](https://bcs.mit.edu/directory/pawan-sinha) are co-leading research that’s measuring AI’s near- and long-term effects on cognition.

Meeting at the intersection of AI, education, and neuroscience, the professors are examining whether generative AI is increasing the human brain’s consumption of information but offloading cognitive function, or supporting an increase in cognitive function when used as part of the creative process. They recently gathered experts on the topic for an event on the MIT campus, “[AI and the Brain](https://mithic.mit.edu/how-does-ai-impact-your-brain/).”

In the field of arts and technology, [Anna Huang](https://www.eecs.mit.edu/people/cheng-zhi-anna-huang/), a professor of music technology holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, [Joe Paradiso](https://www.media.mit.edu/people/joep/overview/), a professor at the MIT Media Lab, are examining how incorporating AI impacts the creative process and live performance experience.

Their project, “Live Musician-AI Improvisation, Tuning the Social Aesthetics in Human-AI Partnerships” explores the question: what happens when human composers and contemporary machine learning systems improvise to make music together?

As part of their project, a collective of MIT musicians, ethnomusicologists, and engineers meets for regular sessions to experiment with improvisation frameworks like stopping to discuss how technology impacts authorship and musical direction, ensemble dynamics, and other cornerstones of improvisation. Faculty will ultimately incorporate their takeaways into a future course or practicum on AI-improvisation.

**Teaching and scholarship in an AI era**

SHASS faculty and academic staff are also leading new MITHIC initiatives to help broaden instruction and community dialogue about the intersection of AI and society.

[Graham Jones](https://anthropology.mit.edu/people/faculty/graham-jones), professor of anthropology, and [Arvind Satyanarayan](https://www.eecs.mit.edu/people/arvind-satyanarayan/), associate professor of computer science, used MITHIC’s SHASS+ Connectivity funding to help launch a course, [6.S061/21A.S02 (Humane User Experience Design)](https://anthropology.mit.edu/21A.S02_21A.S10_Humane_User_Experience_Design), in which students examine how AI systems are designed and grapple with the consequences of AI agents entering into socio-cultural relationships with people through their ability to mimic human thought and speech.

“The crux of our collaboration is the term 'humane.' It’s a bit of a double-entendre, meaning both human-serving or benevolent, and humanlike,” Jones said at the [inaugural MITHIC Annual Event](https://youtu.be/GOToub5Mm8Q?si=mynDMTCtP3-sxlcH). “What’s interesting is that our students are discovering that there’s a fundamental tension between building a system that’s good for people and one that seems human, because real people can develop dangerous dependencies.”

Another project, “Rebuilding Computing and Society at MIT,” is supported by MITHIC’s Education Impact Fund (EIF). Led by [Dwai Banerjee](https://sts-program.mit.edu/people/sts-faculty/dwai-banerjee/), associate professor of science, technology, and society, the initiative revitalized the [Computing and Society concentration](https://shass.mit.edu/for-students/undergraduate-study/computing-and-society-concentration/) launched in 2019. The HASS concentration had gone dormant, listing classes no longer being offered and with minimal student interest. The concentration now features current classes across 11 SHASS units in which students can explore computing through different humanistic and social science angles.

Banerjee, who serves as the concentration’s advisor, is also working with lecturer and research affiliate [Mariel Garcia-Montes PhD ’26](https://cmsw.mit.edu/profile/mariel-garcia-montes/) to find ways to connect the concentration instructors and campus initiatives on computing and society. MIT senior Daniel Gonzalez is also part of the project, developing a research and outreach program that centers undergraduate voices in computing and society efforts across the Institute.

Another MITHIC project funded by the EIF, “Review of Generative AI Assistive and Resistant Communication Assignments and Supporting Workshops,” is led by [Michael Trice](https://cmsw.mit.edu/profile/michael-trice/), a lecturer in MIT’s [Writing, Rhetoric, and Professional Communication (WRAP) program.](https://cmsw.mit.edu/academics/writing-rhetoric-professional-communication/)

The project is responding to a consistent SHASS faculty request for additional training and skills needed “to fully address generative AI concerns in their classes.”

Trice is creating a bank of faculty resources and facilitating workshops and visiting lectures on generative AI and writing. These include a [talk](https://youtu.be/CV-S6_jGauc?si=fH9OrRfXQi_JV4Ag) given earlier this fall by John Gallagher from the University of Illinois, who presented findings from a large-scale survey on AI-usage and writing conducted with undergraduates at his institution in 2026.

**Meeting the moment**

MIT leaders agree that MITHIC, now in its third year, is playing a central role in the Institute meeting the moment, as AI presents both extraordinary potential and disturbing risks.

“There has never been a more important time for constructive collaboration between science and technology and the human-centered disciplines,” MIT President Sally Kornbluth recently said. “Through MITHIC, MIT is giving faculty the support to reach out across disciplines and pursue their dreams.”

Agustín Rayo, dean of SHASS and co-chair of MITHIC, agrees. “MIT is uniquely placed to help us understand this extraordinary moment and to generate the values, tools, and policies that we will need to shape AI so that it becomes a force for good,” he said. “It is essential that we deploy AI technology in a way that elevates human existence, rather than diminishing it.”

At the recent SHASS 75th Anniversary Symposium, Provost Anantha Chandrakasan said given the rapid development of AI, an understanding of the ethical implications and societal impact of implementing new technologies is especially urgent.

“SHASS provides an essential perspective on questions concerning how technology can be developed thoughtfully and deployed responsibly, with the aim of improving human well-being,” said Chandrakasan, who also serves as MITHIC co-chair.

Looking ahead, MITHIC and SERC are developing a series of events that pair humanists or social scientists with colleagues in a single field, starting with mathematics, to examine what AI is changing about how that field produces knowledge and trains its next generation.

“The question isn’t whether AI will change these fields,” Mnookin said. “It’s whether we understand what’s at stake before it does.”

items.articleBody:
## ALEXIS DORNIER ORGANIZES VILLA NABU THROUGH ITS ROOFLINE

In the coastal development of Tampah Hills, South Lombok, [Indonesia](https://www.designboom.com/tag/residential-architecture-interiors/), architect [Alexis Dornier](https://www.designboom.com/tag/architecture-in-indonesia/) has designed Villa Nabu, a 460-square-meter [residence](https://www.designboom.com/tag/residential-architecture-interiors/) defined by a sequence of pitched roofs. Completed in 2024, the house sits on an elevated hillside overlooking the ocean, with a series of adjoining volumes arranged beneath a roofline that rises and falls along the length of the building.

The roof follows the internal organization of the house, with each pitched section corresponding to an individual bedroom. At the right-hand end, the final volume accommodates the main living area, where the ceiling rises to double height. The repetition of the roof forms creates a continuous profile, while their varying spatial functions break the uniformity of the arrangement. From outside, the roof gives away more of the floor plan than most facades do.

Villa Nabu is located in South Lombok | images courtesy of [Alexis Dornier](https://alexisdornier.com/)

## PITCHED ROOFS RESPOND TO LOMBOK’S TROPICAL CLIMATE

The house is positioned to take advantage of the site’s coastal views, with large glazed facades opening the individual volumes toward the surrounding landscape. [Alexis Dornier](https://alexisdornier.com/architecture/) incorporates extended eaves and deep thresholds to provide shaded areas around the building, reducing direct exposure to the tropical sun. These elements also form part of the project’s passive cooling strategy, using the building’s geometry to moderate the relationship between interior spaces and the outdoor climate.

Local stone, timber, and warm-toned finishes make up the material palette. The stone surfaces and timber elements introduce different textures beneath the pitched roof structures, while the glazed openings create visual connections between the rooms and their surroundings. The materials were selected with the intention of weathering over time, and the use of extended roof edges provides additional protection for the facades.

pitched roofs extend along the length of the residence

## VILLA NABU CONNECTS INTERIOR SPACES WITH OUTDOOR TERRACES

Inside, the layout combines open-plan communal areas with more enclosed bedroom spaces. The double-height living room occupies the largest of the roofed volumes and extends toward outdoor terraces and landscaped gardens. Glazing provides views across the hillside, while the transitions between interior and exterior allow the living spaces to open toward the landscape. Bares Furniture and Dua Lighting are credited with the interior design elements.

The residential project includes a 380-square-meter main house, a 40-square-meter guest house, and 40 square meters of back-of-house space. Additional outdoor areas are listed for both the main residence and guest accommodation. Construction is dated to 2021, with completion recorded in 2024. Villa Nabu forms part of the wider Tampah Hills development, where the hillside location and coastal setting inform the orientation and arrangement of the buildings.

items.articleBody:
Angie Nixon speaking at a rally in Kissimmee, Florida. Joe Raedle/Getty Images.

Eight years ago, Democrats retook the U.S. House, [netting 41 seats and winning the national popular vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_elections) by 8.6 points in a textbook blue wave. But despite the rosy national environment, Republican [Rick Scott narrowly defeated incumbent Democratic Senator Bill Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_Senate_election_in_Florida) in Florida. In hindsight, that victory, on the heels of Donald Trump’s 2016 win in the state, was the harbinger of a [death spiral for Florida Democrats](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida) that had begun years earlier.

When I [wrote about the Sunshine State back in February](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida), the consensus from both prediction markets and the experts I spoke with was that Democrats were highly unlikely to win the state in 2026. After a decade of losses and underinvestment, it looked like it could take another ten years for Democrats to turn Florida purple again. The short-term goal of the Florida Democratic Party (FDP) was less “win the 2026 Senate race” and more “[get out of the](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida) *[superminority](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida)* [in the state legislature](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida).”

But back then, no one knew that [2026 would be a blue tsunami](https://www.natesilver.net/p/after-an-extraordinary-wave-what) where Democrats would win the national popular vote by 13 points and net *nine* Senate seats.1 And yet they still lost both statewide races in Florida. Almost immediately, people started posting [post-election recriminations](https://x.com/hollyotterbein/status/2117796466551066896) that if Democrats had spent more in Florida, they could have pulled off at least one win.

So did Democrats blow a golden opportunity in Florida? Or is the state still too tough a target? That question should weigh on the party because in two short years, [Ashley Moody will be up for re-election](https://www.natesilver.net/p/an-extremely-unofficial-first-look).

[↗ natesilver.net](https://www.natesilver.net/p/did-democrats-blow-it-in-florida)

items.articleBody:
*What tracks get Dave Seaman moving? We asked him.*

Dave Seaman has been a fixture of dance music for close to 40 years. As one half of Brothers in Rhythm he co-wrote and produced Kylie Minogue's 'Confide in Me', the record that marked her break from Stock Aitken Waterman pop, and his remix and production credits take in Pet Shop Boys, New Order, Michael Jackson and David Bowie. Alongside that sits a long DJ career built on Global Underground mixes, his *Back to Mine* compilation and Selador, the label he co-runs with Steve Parry.

Remarkably, he has never released a solo studio album until now. [Mirrorball Sleaze](https://found.ee/MirrorballSleaze) landed on Selador on 13 November. With the album now out, we put our Top Tracks questions to him.

### What's the first album you ever bought?

Blondie – [Parallel Lines](https://www.beatport.com/release/parallel-lines/5216975?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c). If you were a ten-year-old boy in 1978, Debbie Harry was particularly alluring.

### The first time you remember hearing electronic music?

Tubeway Army – ['Are "Friends" Electric?'](https://www.beatport.com/track/are-friends-electric/13256328?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c). Gary Numan had a huge impact on me and started a lifelong obsession with synth music.

### Your favourite ever album?

That's a tough one, but if pushed, I'd probably have to say Prince – [Sign o' the Times](https://www.beatport.com/release/sign-o-the-times/6752625?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

### The guaranteed floor-filler?

Donna Summer – ['I Feel Love'](https://www.beatport.com/track/i-feel-love/15739558?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c). Unbelievably, it's 50 years old next year!

### The best tune from last year?

From 2025? DJ Koze – ['Buschtaxi'](https://www.beatport.com/track/buschtaxi/20017608?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

### The guilty pleasure?

Olivia Rodrigo.

### The last track of the night?

That very much depends on the context. Too many variables. Early night or late night? Where and with whom? The occasion?

### The best chillout record?

The remit for my *Back to Mine* compilation was literally to collate some of my favourite chillout tracks, all mixed together on one album, so…

### The record everyone loves, but you hate?

Robin S – ['Show Me Love'](https://www.beatport.com/track/show-me-love/1051600?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

### The best record for a family party?

Earth, Wind & Fire – ['September'](https://www.beatport.com/track/september/11758082?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

### The soundtrack to a lazy Sunday afternoon?

Sade – ['Pearls'](https://www.beatport.com/track/pearls/4789376?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c), poolside at Pikes Ibiza.

### The worst record you've ever heard?

I try to banish those from my mind as soon as I've heard them.

### The record you're proudest of?

Kylie Minogue – ['Confide in Me'](https://www.beatport.com/release/confide-in-me/5832405?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

### The future classic?

DJ Koze – ['Buschtaxi'](https://www.beatport.com/track/buschtaxi/20017608?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

**Find Dave Seaman on [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/daveseamandj/?hl=en) and [Soundcloud.](https://soundcloud.com/daveseaman)**

**Dave Seaman's Mirrorball Sleaze is out on Selador**.**[Listen and buy here](https://www.beatport.com/release/mirrorball-sleaze/7618002?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).**
