items.articleBody:
Policymakers, technologists, and members of the public have raised concerns about the harm AI’s rapid advancement might cause to society. Their concerns include bias, data privacy violations, the spread of misinformation, and losing control of AI agents.

Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems.

In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity.

Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens, who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030. And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow.

“Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.”

Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced.

This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website, a podcast series, and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact.

Eight guiding principles

The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality, but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to offer actionable recommendations for engineers developing AI tools.

The report established eight foundational general principles for designing autonomous and intelligent systems: respecting human rights, prioritizing increased well-being as success criteria for development, empowering individuals with data agency to have control over their identity, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, awareness of misuse, and competence for the system creators.

The principles shift applied ethics to the design stage of AI systems, compared with being a concern after they’re released, the authors wrote.

A suite of standards

The IEEE 7000 series of standards has been developed based on EAD’s framework. Currently the series consists of 29 projects, 11 of which have been published, and more are still being added. They cover topics such as ethical system design model process (IEEE 7000-2021), AI system transparency (IEEE 7001-2021), data privacy (IEEE 7002-2022), algorithmic bias considerations (IEEE 7003-2024), the impact on people’s well-being (IEEE 7010-2020), machine-readable personal privacy requirements (IEEE 7012-2025), and systems that mimic human empathy (IEEE 7014-2024).

AI ethics certifications

IEEE SA offers a suite of ethics in AI programs including IEEE CertifAIEd, which includes two certifications: one for individuals and one for products.

The professional certification provides individuals with skills to assess autonomous and intelligent systems for adherence to IEEE’s methodology and ethics criteria.

“Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE.” —John C. Havens, founding executive director of the global initiative

The product certification program assesses whether an organization’s AI tool or system conforms to the criteria in the IEEE Ontological Specifications. A CertifiAIEd assessor evaluates the product to ensure it meets the criteria. Upon completion of the assessment, the owner submits it to the IEEE Conformity Assessment Program, which can certify it and issue the certification mark.

IEEE SA also recently released its Responsible AI for Children certification program. This program certifies that AI products for children have been independently tested and verified to meet design and ethics requirements.

New industry connections group

The IEEE Artificial Intelligence Systems (AIS) for Global Flourishing Collaborative Industry Collections group was formed to provide the resources, knowledge, and tools needed to prioritize people’s well-being to developers of AI systems. It has more than 200 members.

The collaborative describes its work as a practical, systems-level framework for responsible technology design that translates flourishing into applied methods, metrics, and tools that can be used throughout the AIS lifecycle.

The group is establishing guidelines for how to design, evaluate, and govern systems that can measurably improve human well-being and ecological sustainability.

Subcommittees are focused on cognition, education, faith, planetary care, spirituality, and other issues.

“The group is building directly off the well-being chapter of Ethically Aligned Design and the IEEE 7010 standard (Recommended Practice for Assessing the Impact of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems on Human Well-Being),” Havens says. “That’s on purpose because if human and planetary flourishing aren’t addressed first in design, then human well-being and planetary sustainability are afterthoughts.”

Podcasts and blogs

To mark the 10-year anniversary, IEEE SA created the five-part “Ethically Aligned Design: 10 Years of Impact” podcast series. It launched on 21 October. New episodes are being released every two weeks.

The episodes center around the vision for EAD, the process for selecting its foundational principles, and how they were translated into the IEEE 7000 standards.

The first podcast, “Origins of Ethically Aligned Design,” explored early efforts to make ethics a practical part of AI and autonomous system design. The experts discussed challenges, debates, global collaboration, and the real-world impact that helped move responsible technology from ethical principles toward actionable standards and practices.

The second podcast, “The Chapters and Committees” focuses on the multidisciplinary groups that worked on turning broad human values into practical guidance for AI and autonomous systems.

The podcast discussions serve as material for a thought leadership program that also includes blog articles about the IEEE 7000 series and educational resources to continue to raise awareness and support of this groundbreaking work.

items.articleBody:
Adam Engst, writing at TidBITS:

> This past August, I did something I had never done before:
> released a full-fledged Mac app. Prompted by tech ghost stories
> about settings mysteriously changing during operating system
> updates, I spent months working with Claude Code to create a
> utility called SetShot that would reveal what settings change
> during macOS updates (see “[SetShot Tracks macOS Settings Changes](https://tidbits.com/2026/08/19/setshot-tracks-macos-settings-changes/),” 19 August 2026). So far, I haven’t caught Apple
> red-handed, although I still hear chatter about configuration
> changes after users install updates.
> Practically speaking, SetShot offers something never previously
> available to Mac users: the capability to identify and log
> settings changes over time, whether made by you, macOS, or some
> app. To that end, it takes and compares snapshots of numerous
> settings deep within macOS, reporting on what changed between
> them. It never changes any settings, so the worst it can do is
> tell you something you didn’t want to know.

[SetShot](https://tidbits.com/setshot/) is a very cool app, and so very Adam Engst-flavored. Free of charge and [open source](https://github.com/adamengst/setshot-app) to boot.

There’s an anecdote involving me in Engst’s post, and while SetShot couldn’t fix my problem directly, it was very helpful in showing me where to look to fix it myself. The backstory: I set a custom “Text highlight color” in System Preferences: Appearances many years ago — I mean like maybe 20 years ago — and had not changed it in years. It’s just the perfect shade of blue. But one night two months ago I went screwing around to see what the modern default text highlight colors are, and, son of a bitch, when I tried to change my color back to the custom one I’d been using for decades, I couldn’t. The way the color picker stores color values from the modern Appearance settings panel must have changed. It still honors the old value I had if it’s in the defaults system that way, but it writes a different style of value if you change it in the Appearance panel in System Settings.

Here’s a short version of how I got my old color back. Using System Settings, I changed the custom color to the exact RGB values 0.2 / 0.4 / 0.6. Then I read them from the command line:

❯ defaults read -g AppleHighlightColor
0.200000 0.400000 0.600000 Other

That’s not the color I wanted; I just wanted to prove that that’s the global key for a custom text highlight color. When I read those same values from a backup version of my *~/Library/Preferences/.GlobalPreferences.plist* file (always have backups, kids), with my beloved custom color, it looked liked this:

❯ defaults read /path/to/.GlobalPreferences.plist AppleHighlightColor
0.698039 0.760784 0.835294

So the old value was a string with three floating point RGB values. The new value was a string with those three values *plus* the word “Other”. This command, writing back my custom RGB values without the word “Other”:

❯ defaults write -g AppleHighlightColor "0.698039 0.760784 0.835294"

restored the color I’ve been using since George W. Bush was still president. It’s a really good color, trust me.

[★](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/17/setshot-1-0)

items.articleBody:
[Nendo](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/nendo/) has selected [Linde Freya Tangelder](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/linde-freya-tangelder/) for Dezeen's [20×20](https://www.dezeen.com/20x20) project in partnership with [Kohler](https://www.studiokohler.com/collections?id=Paidmedia_Dezeen_Kohler_International-20anni_2026_brand_version-1). In this [interview](https://www.dezeen.com/interviews/), the Dutch designer explains why she doesn't find design inspiring.

Insofar as she creates furniture and lighting, Tangelder is technically a designer, but only just.

"How I think is not typical design," she told Dezeen. "So I'm never thinking about function in the first place. The whole process is very intuitive, it's just a cloud of connections in my head – more about concepts or stories that I want to tell rather than making a functional piece."

"I've never been so inspired by design in general," she added. "It's a skill that fits very well to me, but I'd rather connect it in inspiration to art, to architecture, or another discipline."

With a highly sculptural style, Tangelder also sometimes refers to herself as an artist – a label she says she wouldn't have dared use when starting out.

She has made a name for herself through pieces that often play with unexpected juxtapositions of materials and use traditional methods of production to create an unmistakably contemporary aesthetic.

"I like to use poor materials, rich materials, and fuse them," she explained. "For me, it's sort of a synonym for how I think culture should be."

Tangelder is known for sculptural pieces that play with unusual material combinations. Photo by Alejandro Ramirez Orozco

In 2019, she was [identified by Dezeen as a young designer to watch](https://www.dezeen.com/2019/03/23/young-designers-collectible-2019/) after exhibiting at [Collectible](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/collectible/), as well as winning that year's [Biennale Interieur](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/biennale-interieur/) designer of the year award.

Explaining the studio's decision to select her as a 20x20 nomination, Nendo praised Tangelder's approach for being "both remarkably gentle and quietly bold".

Among her notable pieces is the Bolder Chair. Photo by Alexander Popelier

"Driven by a playful curiosity to take architecture apart and put it back together, she reveals qualities in familiar materials that we have long overlooked," the studio told Dezeen.

Referencing buildings in the medium of furniture has become something of a calling card for Tangelder.

Notable examples include the Bolder Chair, which recalls architectural columns, the Windows of Bo Bardi table, which mimics the shape of windows on the SESC Pompéia Factory in São Paulo, and Brick’s Reflection Chair with its terracotta backrest (pictured left).

These propensities are reflected evocatively in the name of Tangelder's studio – [Destroyers/Builders](https://destroyersbuilders.com/) – though recently, she tends to work more under her own name.

"I'm inspired by architecture, things I see in buildings," she said. "I think it's just really interesting to scale it down to the field of artistic design, or limited-edition design."

"In the history of architecture there's so much to tell," she continued. "For me it's more diverse and also less superficial than the history of design, and I think that's what interests me so much."

"And also that it feels more essential, I think that is maybe the core. I just like brick. I like simple materials that are used for construction rather than smooth finishes just for decoration."

Her home and studio are just outside Brussels. Photo by Eline Willaert

Not that she is completely opposed to smooth, decorative finishes – as evidenced by the fact that an entire room in the home-slash-studio that she shares with her landscape-architect partner is used exclusively for lacquering.

In fact, most of the house, which is in a leafy area outside Brussels, is taken up by Tangelder's atelier space.

She moved to [Belgium](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/belgium/) shortly after graduating from [Design Academy Eindhoven](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/design-academy-eindhoven/) in 2013, and has become part of an increasingly rich design scene in the country over the past decade.

> In the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing. Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there's so much investment in each project

"I moved to Belgium because I really like the culture, the art scene, architecture as well," said Tangelder. "The design scene I thought was actually quite minimal, or I didn't really see a lot of studios at that time. But I liked that as well, it felt a little bit more new for me."

"I think it developed a lot, the landscape in design in Belgium over the last 10 years," she considered. "There's a lot happening right now."

It has certainly been a productive decade for Tangelder, whose back-catalogue is impressively extensive considering she has only ever employed a very small number of assistants.

Part of that has been made possible thanks to collaborations with the healthy network of craftspeople across Belgium that Tangelder has established to help with production.

"That has been super important for me," she said. "Each material that I really love, I have a partner now."

Tangelder spends nearly every day in the studio. Photo by Mieke Verbeijlen

But moreover, the chunky portfolio is a reflection of a huge amount of hours spent working in the studio. Though she says her work-life balance is improving, Tangelder works almost every day including weekends, and has been known to go years without a holiday.

"I really like it, so for me it's the best way to spend my time," she said, before pausing.

"I should think about it more as fun time, because of course it's also a struggle. You're always struggling over all the decisions that have to be made."

> So that means you take risks all the time. It's maybe more intense, but also more fun

Like many independent designers, Tangelder has had to battle to earn a living from her discipline.

"In the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing," she remembered. "Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there's so much investment in each project."

Over time, she says she has acquired a reasonably good sense of which pieces are likely to prove more lucrative, though she has resisted the temptation to focus her energies entirely on these.

"I think when you decide to only continue projects that you know will have commercial success, then it will be less experimental," she explained.

"So that means you take risks all the time," she added. "It's maybe more intense, but also more fun."

A solo exhibition at this year's Milan design week showcased Tangelder's one-off pieces alongside her products for Cassina. Photo by Eline Willaert

Most of Tangelder's work involves one-off or limited-edition pieces for galleries, but she has also partnered with brands.

A big moment came in 2022 when she was commissioned by [Cassina](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/cassina/) to produce a collection of side tables and pouffes, and she has continued to work with the Italian brand each year since.

This year she was able to put on [a solo exhibition at Milan design week](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/05/06/linde-freya-tangelder-crafts-fluid-re-collection/) supported by Cassina, showcasing a combination of her independent pieces and products created for the brand.

> I just think the material is very me. That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It's really in between a sculpture and a functional object

It was an unusual example of small-scale making and larger-scale production design being displayed side-by-side.

Far from being a barrier to creative expression, Tangelder has found that these commissions can be an enabler by providing up-front revenues, unlike solo work.

"So it gives less pressure, I would say, which is very good for the creative process," she said.

But you can have too much of a good thing, and while she enjoys the more collaborative experience of working for a brand she limits this type of work to two projects per year to ensure she has plenty of time for her own pieces.

Tangelder's current obsession is cast and oxidised metal, so she reports spending a lot of time these days in a foundry in Antwerp. Her most recent piece is a grungy take on a conventional desk lamp, in white bronze.

"I just think the material is very me," she remarked. "That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It's really in between a sculpture and a functional object."

A recently created desk lamp is among Tangelder's favourite of her own pieces. Photo courtesy of Linde Freya Tangelder

Looking to the future, she is interested in working more with fashion, having previously designed a chair for [Dior](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/dior/).

And, she would like to work on a larger-scale installation – perhaps an outdoor sculpture, she suggests.

In a world where for various reasons the boundary between design and art is increasingly blurred, Tangelder is undoubtedly at the forefront.

She is an interesting 20/20 choice from Sato, who is typically associated with minimalist, highly functional product design.

For her part, Tangelder sees her work as partly an indirect response to the Sato approach – a continuation of a conversation.

"I have, of course, quite a different form language, but I think it's also a reaction to what he's done," she said.

"He's so clear in the decisions that he makes, he's a master in it, and I'm really grateful that he sees what I've been doing."

*The main photo is by* *[Alexander Popelier](https://www.instagram.com/alexanderpopelier/?hl=en-gb).*

- ### 20x20 To celebrate Dezeen's 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we'll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. [Click here to explore](https://www.dezeen.com/20x20)

items.articleBody:
Tripod for iPhone.

Over the years, I’ve realized that I’m a particular type of podcast listener: I do not listen to every single new episode that comes in from the shows I’m subscribed to; I want to see them in a list, then pick and choose the episodes I want, and arrange them in a queue. The interactions need to be simple and the queue tactile, ideally with drag and drop to move specific episodes up and down. I do not personally care about transcripts and video (although [we support both with our shows](https://www.macstories.net/news/macstories-podcasts-now-let-you-switch-between-video-and-audio-in-apple-podcasts/), and I think they’re great additions). I do not need an Apple Watch app. I do not need playlists. And I want to have audio effects – pioneered by [Marco Arment in Overcast](https://marco.org/apps), now found in the most popular indie podcast apps – to trim silence and boost volume. I listen to most podcasts at 1.5x speed, but some at 1.8x. I play podcasts from my iPhone, and I want to use an *extremely* native app that also comes with a CarPlay version.

The intersection of all these preferences is surprisingly hard to find in a single, well-rounded iPhone app. I find [Overcast](https://overcast.fm/) to have the best audio effects and performance, but I do not understand its queuing system. For the longest time, I used [Pocket Casts](https://pocketcasts.com/), but the design wasn’t great, and it was often slow at refreshing my feeds. I would have used [Castro](https://castro.fm/), which had the closest version of the queue management system I wanted, but the app’s future has always been somewhat up in the air…and [it just changed ownership, again](https://mjtsai.com/blog/2026/11/06/castro-sold-yet-again/).

With this context in mind, you can imagine my surprise when, seemingly out of the blue, [indie developer Ben McCarthy](https://benricemccarthy.com/apps/) – a [longtime friend of MacStories](https://www.macstories.net/?s=Ben%20McCarthy) and wildly proficient iOS developer – dropped [Tripod](https://benricemccarthy.com/tripod/), their brand new podcast app designed around an inbox and queue system.

I’ll cut to the chase: Tripod is the best podcast app I’ve tried in a long time. The app looks wonderful on the iPhone Duo, it has the best-designed and most reasonable (for my brain, at least) inbox-queue combo I’ve seen to date, and it is full of little details, hidden Easter eggs, and small quality-of-life features that make it a remarkable option for Castro expats and, for my taste, one of the best app debuts of 2026.

The idea behind Tripod is pretty simple: there is an inbox and a queue. New episodes land in the inbox, which you can configure in terms of notifications, UI (you can optionally show action buttons underneath each episode, or rely on the default context menu for managing them), and behavior. For instance, you can choose to automatically remove episodes older than one week or one month, or just keep a specific number of a show’s recent episodes.

Tripod’s inbox screen.

Immediately in the inbox, there are some details I appreciate. When you long-press to show the context menu for a podcast, the menu items are tinted to match the key color of the podcast’s artwork, which is a lovely detail. But also in this menu, you can choose to either remove an episode or mark it as played (not a lot of apps get this right!), jump to the podcast’s main page, and either add it to the queue or ‘Someday’ list (more on this later).

Menu items are tinted per podcast.

In the inbox, you can group episodes by date or show – the latter option being especially effective if you just want to see how many inbox episodes you have for a specific podcast in your library, so you can quickly triage them. Speaking of the library: you can long-press a show to easily choose where new episodes should land from a context menu, but you can also tweak a podcast’s dedicated settings. These include notifications as well as separate limits for the inbox and queue.

You’ll also notice a scrollable list of filters at the top of the library. These UI elements are available on this page as well as the queue, but I find them to be best suited for the queue, where they make the most sense to me. The queue is a list of episodes where, as previously seen in Castro, episodes can be delightfully rearranged with drag and drop. Various grouping and sorting options are available here as well, but it’s the filter row at the top that I love. With filters, you can sort Tripod’s queue by in-progress episodes (boring, but necessary), favorites, and my three favorite options: short episodes, episodes by category, and “someday” episodes.

Tripod’s queue.

With the ‘Short’ filter, I can quickly get through episodes that don’t last too long; categories are fetched from Apple Podcasts’ database, and they’re an ingenious way to triage episodes based on what I’m in the mood for without having to create smart playlists upfront (something I used to do in Pocket Casts). The ‘Someday’ list (which seems to be inspired by [the namesake feature originally seen in Things](https://culturedcode.com/things/support/articles/4001304/)) is a surprisingly useful way to save evergreen episodes I know I want to get to, well, *someday*, but don’t have to be part of my daily rotation. For example, [Myke Hurley’s ‘State of the Workflow’ series](https://www.theenthusiast.net/state-of-the-workflow/) on [Cortex](https://relay.fm/cortex) is perfect for the Someday list since those episodes aren’t time-sensitive or news-heavy, and hold their value months after their release date.

Filters in the queue.

The result of all these decisions is that when I spend time interacting with Tripod, everything clicks and works with the way my brain thinks of managing podcasts. The app is also a great example of how to design for the iPhone Duo: every device pose is supported, and when the Duo is unfolded, the Now Playing screen lives in a left sidebar so you can both navigate the app and manage your listening session.

Different iPhone Duo poses for Tripod.

Features seen in other podcast apps are also seen here: swipe up on the artwork, and you’ll get pages in the sidebar for chapters (you can select which ones you want to skip), a real-time transcript (which is generated on-device and seems comparable to Overcast’s in terms of quality), and audio settings.

Pages in Tripod’s Now Playing screen, including the ability to generate clips for social media.

And it is, in fact, when comparing Tripod to Overcast that I need to air some of my complaints about this early version of the app (Tripod launched last week, and a 2026.4 update – which I tested for this review – is launching soon on the App Store). Tripod does not support streaming episodes yet, and it’s a download-only affair for now. That is not a dealbreaker for me, but I don’t care about keeping episodes offline and dislike having to wait a few seconds before an episode begins, so I hope McCarthy supports streaming in the near future. Second, while Tripod does have audio effects for trimming silence between words and adjusting volume (it’s an equalizer with different options), they don’t sound nearly as good as Marco Arment’s effects to my ears. Arment has been tweaking and optimizing those effects for years, and it shows. That said, Tripod’s effects are certainly better than some sloppy podcast clients I’ve tried this year, and they get the job done.

What Tripod may lack in maturity (the app is not on the iPad or Mac either, for example), it compensates for with fun details that are a testament to McCarthy’s taste and deep knowledge of iOS. Promo codes for sponsors are automatically extracted from episodes you listen to and their show notes, and made available for quick copy in the Search screen. Links you open from show notes are also temporarily saved, so you can easily find them later. There are two stunning Six Colors and Trans alternative app icons; you can review your entire activity in the app in a dedicated screen; and there are listening stats that – I have to assume – will be made easier to share, Spotify Wrapped-style, at some point.

Tripod can automatically find promo codes for sponsors of your favorite shows.

It’s always been hard to stand out in the App Store, but even more so these days because of the [increasing number of new app releases](https://www.macstories.net/linked/app-store-chaos/) made possible by AI coding agents. However, as someone who’s been doing this for 17 years, I can tell you that – and excuse my French – it’s still quite easy to tell a shitty app apart from one that is thoughtful, designed with care, and considered with the restraint that is necessary to ship a quality product.

[Tripod](https://benricemccarthy.com/tripod/) is both the sum of its parts and the parts it *doesn’t* have. It’s an opinionated podcast app created for a particular type of podcast listener that, however, pulls off the tricky balancing act of blending its creator’s opinions with customization features for a wider audience.

If you’re the kind of person who would enjoy listening to podcasts with this kind of app, I think [you already know what to do](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tripod-podcast-player/id6824844745).
items.body: Tripod for iPhone. The interactions need to be simple and the queue tactile, ideally with drag and drop to move specific episodes up and down. I do not personally care about transcripts and video (although we support both with our shows, and I think they’re great additions). I do not need an Apple Watch app. I do not need playlists. And I want to have audio effects – pioneered by Marco Arment in Overcast, now found in the most popular indie podcast apps – to trim silence and boost volume. I listen to most podcas…

items.articleBody:
### 💬 Jensen Huang says he’s willing to return as Nvidia CEO

[↗ Primärquelle: techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/17/jensen-huang-says-he-would-be-honored-if-allowed-to-return-as-nvidia-ceo/)

- Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia's founder and CEO, said in his first public statement since leaving that he would be honored to return to the top job if the board decides it serves the company's interest.
- Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1 and said he is committed to cooperating with the board's independent investigation, while Nvidia formed a new executive committee to oversee export control compliance.
- An open letter calling for his return drew over 10,000 current and former Nvidia staff plus figures like Elon Musk, but a board source told the Washington Post yesterday there were no plans to reinstate him.

### 🦹 Popular websites subverted in bid to steal crypto

[↗ Primärquelle: firstpost.com](https://www.firstpost.com/tech/popular-websites-subverted-in-bid-to-steal-crypto-target-iphone-users-14060570.html)

- Attackers planted malicious JavaScript on the websites of 178 organizations, including Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce and IKEA, trying to steal cryptocurrency and infect iPhones, security researcher Scott Helme said yesterday.
- The scripts reached visitors through Optimizely, a website optimization platform, and tried to swap crypto payment addresses with the attacker's wallet, skim credit card numbers, grab cookies and screenshots, and drop exploit code onto iOS devices.
- Salesforce said it was investigating unauthorized Optimizely script changes and disabled them as a precaution, while Equifax looked into the problem, stopped using Optimizely, and reported no evidence that its systems were compromised.

### 📱 Meta launches Direct, a standalone messaging app

[↗ Primärquelle: engadget.com](https://www.engadget.com/2318452/meta-is-testing-direct-a-standalone-messaging-app-for-instagram/)

- Meta has begun testing Direct, a standalone Instagram messaging app that pulls the photo-sharing service's inbox into its own app and, notably, lets people use it without an Instagram account.
- Direct mirrors Instagram's inbox layout and carries over existing chats, Notes, and custom thread backgrounds, but people who sign up with just an email or phone number must add contacts manually through a username or QR code.
- Available only in Thailand and Turkey for now, Direct blocks chats with unconnected accounts, lets parents monitor teens through Meta's controls, and claims technology to spot inappropriate interactions with young users.

### 🛡️ Nvidia forms export-control board after Huang exit

[↗ Primärquelle: theregister.com](https://www.theregister.com/systems/2026/11/17/nvidia-places-chip-exports-under-boardroom-supervision-after-huangs-exit/5310429)

- Nvidia's board has set up a national security and export control committee following the resignation of co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang and claims that Singapore customer Megaspeed sent GPUs to China.
- Chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, the panel will meet at least quarterly to watch Nvidia's export compliance and trade risks, with existing compliance teams reporting to it and interim CEO Colette Kress.
- Huang quit last week after admitting an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US authorities reportedly suspected of working for Chinese intelligence, while Commerce and Justice confirmed they had been investigating Megaspeed since 2024.

### 🔐 macOS warns against giving AI apps full Mac control

[↗ Primärquelle: macrumors.com](https://www.macrumors.com/2026/11/16/macos-27-3-full-desk-access/)

- Apple's macOS 27.3 beta gives Mac users tighter control over what apps can touch, with new safeguards aimed at AI agent apps that could expose files, mail, messages, and browsing history.
- Apple is splitting the old Device Control and Data Access setting into System & App Protection Override and Accessibility, and will push users to grant access only to the specific apps or folders a task actually needs.
- Users can set apps to ask each time instead of handing over blanket access, and a menu bar indicator will appear whenever a requesting app is controlling another app through System & App Protection Override.

### 🛡️ OpenAI gives 24-hour bans for child abuse prompts

[↗ Primärquelle: techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/openai-releases-a-new-image-classifier-and-chatgpt-warnings-to-combat-csam/)

- OpenAI rolled out new tools today to fight child sexual abuse material, including warning screens in ChatGPT that suspend accounts for 24 hours when users try prompts aimed at sexualizing children.
- A new image classifier, built with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, detects abuse images including AI-generated ones, and in testing flagged 48% fewer images while catching the same number of abusive ones.
- Repeated offenses could get accounts removed for good, and OpenAI is sharing the classifier free through its API with select companies while publishing child-safety guidelines for developers and giving law enforcement investigative tools.

### 🧰 Trending tools

**AirOps:** 48% of AI search citations come from community platforms. Their 2026 report breaks down how modern brands stay visible in AI search. [Get the free report](https://go.dupple.com/lg-techpresso-airops-iyyfu4)

**Wine-Assembly:** runs unmodified Windows 98.exe files in-browser via an x86 interpreter and Win32 API reimplementation written in WebAssembly Text. [↗ wine-assembly.berrry.app](https://wine-assembly.berrry.app)

**Zigzag:** a free, open-source native Mac browser built on WebKit that replicates Arc's interface, supports Chrome extensions, and imports existing browser data. [↗ github.com](https://github.com/ZigaoWang/zigzag)

**OpenTodo:** a self-hosted, local-first task manager shipped as a single Go binary, with offline support, natural-language input, time blocking, Pomodoro focus timers, and shared lists across phone, desktop, and 20 platforms. [↗ github.com](https://github.com/OpenTodoApp/OpenTodo)

**Jamaican Flag Font:** a custom font rendering text as flag-inspired glyphs, with a connected variant that matches background colors and joins letters via contextual features. [↗ bobbiec.github.io](https://bobbiec.github.io/jamaican-font.html)

**The Last Complication:** a Zachtronics-style puzzle game about watchmaking, where players solve mechanical complications through counter-movement rules across a board-based system. [↗ lastcomplication.com](https://lastcomplication.com)

**T1DMAI:** trains and benchmarks 15 blood glucose forecasting models, including a small transformer that predicts glucose two hours ahead for research use. [↗ github.com](https://github.com/0xdeadf1sh/T1DMAI)

items.title: Helen Garner Will Receive Our 2027 Hadada Award
items.subtitle: In the early seventies, Helen Garner and her two-year-old daughter moved into a communal house of mostly single mothers in the inner suburbs of Mel…

items.articleBody:
Photograph by Darren James.

In the early seventies, Helen Garner and her two-year-old daughter moved into a communal house of mostly single mothers in the inner suburbs of Melbourne, the first of several share homes they would live in during that decade. The house was noisy and chaotic but offered Garner a creative freedom that she hadn’t found in her first marriage. While her daughter played with the other children, Garner read Proust and Tolstoy, wrote in her diary, and began a passionate love affair with a man who was addicted to heroin. As the relationship went on, she began to see her experiences as a narrative. “Story is a chunk of life with a bend in it, and I could feel this one coming,” Garner tells Thessaly La Force in **[The Art of Fiction No. 255](https://www.theparisreview.org/interviews/7929/the-art-of-fiction-no-255-helen-garner)**, published in issue no. 241. “I suddenly thought, Maybe I could write about this while it’s still happening, as it’s coming into its bend.”

The resulting novel, Garner’s debut, *Monkey Grip* (1977), created a rupture in the landscape of Australian literature, winning Garner first prize in the National Book Council Awards while also provoking consternation among critics for its depictions of unconventional domestic life, sex, and female desire. Some accused Garner of merely publishing her journal—which is, in fact, more or less what she had done. In an essay published in 2002, she asked why this should be a bad thing. “As if there were no work involved in keeping a diary in the first place,” she wrote. “It’s as if a diary wrote itself, as if it poured out in a sludgy, involuntary, self-indulgent stream.” (Her extraordinary diaries have been published in three volumes spanning from 1978 to 1998.)

Garner was born in 1942 in the coastal city of Geelong, Victoria, the eldest of six. “In a big family you’ve got to find a way of getting away from everybody to a place where you can quietly exist, and that’s what reading was for me,” she tells La Force. “It was my way of being absent. I used to kneel by the side of my bed so I could keep reading even while I was pulling my clothes on.” The family unit—particularly under strain or in free fall—has frequently been a subject of her novels, including *The Children’s Bach* (1984), in which the circumscribed lives of a couple are upturned by a visit from an old friend’s bohemian family, and *The Spare Room* (2008), in which the narrator hosts an old friend who is undergoing alternative treatment for cancer, and which deals with the frustrations of care with brutal honesty.

Family has been central, too, in Garner’s nonfiction, most notably in two books about her experience of following murder trials: *Joe Cinque’s Consolation* (2004), about a young woman who killed her boyfriend, and *This House of Grief* (2014), about a father who drove himself and his three children into a dam, killing the children. “The thing is, despite being told that my concerns were too domestic, I’ve always known that the family is where everything is played out,” Garner tells La Force.

Over the past five decades, in her fiction, journalism, and essays, Garner has continually brought the fullness of her self to bear on the page: her scrupulous honesty, emotional intelligence, clarity, and imagination. She has been awarded the Windham-Campbell Prize, the Melbourne Prize for Literature, and the Walkley Award, and has been inducted into the Victorian Honour Roll of Women. We are delighted to add to this list the Hadada, our award for lifetime achievement, which has previously been awarded to writers including John Ashbery, Anne Carson, Deborah Eisenberg, Jamaica Kincaid, N. Scott Momaday, Edward P. Jones, and James Salter. We are tremendously excited to present Garner with the Hadada on **[April 6](https://www.theparisreview.org/revel)** at the Spring Revel, our annual gathering of writers, artists, and friends to celebrate and raise funds for the *Review*, which is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. Tickets are now available, and all proceeds from the event will help us continue to seek out the best new work and share it with readers in print and online. We hope you’ll **[join](https://www.theparisreview.org/revel)** us.

items.articleBody:
Midterm results showed that men under 30 (a supposed MAGA bulwark) shifted back to voting mostly for Democrats. Louise Perry and I spoke about whether that signals the end of the New Right.

Among other things, we discuss whether perceptions of corruption played a role. Voters will overlook a president lining his pockets, so long as they themselves feel prosperous. But the economy feels shaky for many people. Moreover, we discuss whether the online right on X made the same mistake the online left made back when it was still called Twitter: confusing applause from fellow partisans with the preferences of normal people.

Louise and I also speak about whether it’s true that “the left can’t meme.” We converge on an answer that involves censorship, 4chan, sex differences in humor, esoteric messaging, and why so much political imagery now looks like it was made for toddlers. We also get into what I heard Dave Chappelle recently say at Madison Square Garden about Charlie Kirk.

Finally, I asked Louise a question every man has wondered about women’s group chats. Her answer was not what I expected.

[↗ robkhenderson.com](https://www.robkhenderson.com/p/did-the-new-right-meme-itself-out)

items.articleBody: Protein–protein interfaces encode molecular recognition through spatially organized contacts, yet their buried, curved surfaces are difficult to inspect as a whole. Flattening these surfaces can expose interface organization but introduces geometric distortion and may divide individual residues into disconnected regions. We present TopoPPI, a geometry-aware platform that converts interaction surfaces into low-distortion two-dimensional atlases while retaining links to source atoms, residues and contacts. TopoPPI extends OptCuts with a contact-weighted penalty for seam-induced fragmentation of residue footprints—the surface regions assigned to individual residues—jointly balancing continuity, seam length and distortion. In a leakage-controlled benchmark of 2,236 experimental complexes, the geometry-only OptCuts foundation achieved 88.39% lower family-weighted scale-fair distortion than the next-best tested parameterization across 2,209 complete comparable outputs. Across 2,204 exact-domain comparisons, TopoPPI reduced family-weighted residue-footprint fragmentation by 12.81% (95% confidence interval, 11.50–14.05%), with a 2.60% increase in normalized seam length and a 0.061% increase in scale-fair distortion. Continuity gains extended to 1,180 fixed-pose pairs of AlphaFold monomer models and 145 predicted complexes, with fragmentation reductions of 18.60% and 11.65%, respectively. Functionally annotated antibody and colicin–immunity interfaces demonstrated reconnection of the footprints of experimentally characterized binding and specificity residues. Further applications mapped published binding and folding free-energy estimates onto the KRAS–RAF1 interface and compared shared receptor residues across two growth-hormone recognition sites. Available through graphical and command-line interfaces, TopoPPI provides a residue-aware visualization framework for integrating structural contacts and functional annotations within geometrically controlled interface maps.

items.articleBody:
A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone. Another sees a peer being excluded from a group chat. Someone knows a friend has been struggling but hesitates before reaching out. Why?

Most adults assume the challenge is getting young people to care. But after spending years studying adolescent compassion, I have come to believe that caring may not be the central problem.

Many adolescents care deeply.

The question is what happens next.

We often imagine compassion as a straightforward process: Notice suffering, feel concern, take action. Yet anyone who has worked with adolescents knows that the path is rarely so simple. Young people are navigating friendships, social hierarchies, identity development, and concerns about belonging, all while learning how to manage their own emotions. In these moments, compassion is not simply a feeling. It is a decision unfolding within a complex social world.

In our [recent research developing the Youth Compassion Measure](https://doi.org/10.1177/01650254261485170), an assessment of compassionate responding, we find that most adolescents recognize when a peer is struggling. What varies is whether that recognition translates into helping. Across hundreds of students, four factors consistently shape whether compassion becomes action: peer dynamics, social risk, emotional regulation, and intrinsic motivation.

Understanding these factors may help parents, educators, and youth-serving professionals better support compassionate action in young people.

## 1. Compassion has to survive peer dynamics

One of the clearest findings from our work is that adolescents were more likely to help when the person experiencing distress was someone they knew well.

At first glance, this may seem obvious. Most of us are more likely to check on a close friend than a stranger. Yet this finding points to a deeper truth about adolescence: Compassion unfolds within relationships.

During adolescence, friendships become central to daily life. Young people are figuring out who they are, where they belong, and how they fit into their social worlds. Relationships provide security, identity, and connection. Unsurprisingly, those same relationships shape compassionate responding.

This means that compassion is not simply an individual trait. It is also social.

When educators talk about creating compassionate schools, they often focus on [teaching empathy or kindness](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/how_educators_are_using_kindness_to_transform_schools). Those efforts matter. But our findings suggest that fostering strong, supportive relationships may be just as important. Young people appear more willing to take compassionate action when they feel connected to the people around them.

In other words, belonging may do more than improve well-being. It may help create the conditions that allow compassion to flourish.

## 2. Compassion involves social risk

If relationships explain who adolescents help, social risk helps explain why they sometimes do not.

Consider a common scenario. A student witnesses a peer being teased. They know the behavior is hurtful. They may even want to intervene. Yet stepping forward could carry consequences. They may worry about being judged, excluded, or embarrassed, or becoming a target themselves.

Our findings suggest that adolescents are often weighing these possibilities, consciously or unconsciously, before deciding how to respond.

This is one reason public conversations about bullying can be so frustrating. When videos circulate online, attention quickly turns to the bystanders. Why didn’t anyone help?

The question assumes that recognizing suffering naturally leads to action. But social reality is more complicated.

Young people are often assessing multiple things at once: the seriousness of the situation, who is involved, who is watching, what might happen if they intervene, and what might happen if they do not. What appears from the outside as indifference may actually be a moment of conflict between compassion and self-protection.

This perspective does not excuse harmful behavior or passivity. But it does encourage us to understand helping as a social act rather than a purely moral one.

If we want young people to act compassionately, we need environments where compassionate action is socially supported instead of socially costly.

## 3. Compassion requires emotional regulation

Perhaps the most surprising finding from our study is that recognizing suffering alone did not consistently predict helping.

Many students understood that someone was struggling. The difference was what happened after that recognition occurred.

One of the strongest predictors of compassionate action is distress tolerance, the ability to remain engaged in the presence of emotional discomfort. This matters because witnessing another person’s suffering is often uncomfortable. We may feel sadness, anxiety, uncertainty, helplessness, or fear of saying the wrong thing. Adolescents experience these emotions, too.

Imagine a teenager whose friend is crying. The challenge is not simply recognizing that the friend is upset; it’s navigating the delicate space between overidentifying with another person’s suffering and distancing oneself from it. Too much emotional absorption can lead to overwhelm and withdrawal. Too much distance can lead to disengagement. Compassion requires something different: remaining connected to another person’s experience while maintaining enough emotional balance to respond effectively.

People sometimes assume that compassion and empathy are the same thing. They are not. [Empathy](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/topic/empathy/definition#what-is-empathy) allows us to resonate with another person’s experience. [Compassion](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/topic/compassion/definition#what-is-compassion) involves channeling that awareness into a desire to alleviate suffering. Doing so requires emotional regulation. Without it, concern can become overwhelm, uncertainty, or avoidance. Instead of moving toward suffering, we move away from it.

Our findings suggest that compassionate action depends not only on recognizing another person’s distress, but also on the ability to stay present with that distress without becoming consumed by it. In this sense, emotional regulation is not separate from compassion; it helps make compassion possible.

For parents and educators, this finding has important practical implications. Teaching young people how to navigate difficult emotions may strengthen their capacity for compassionate action. Skills such as mindfulness, emotional awareness, reflection, and distress tolerance are not simply tools for managing stress. They may also be the very capacities that help adolescents transform caring into action by staying engaged when helping feels uncertain, vulnerable, or emotionally difficult.

## 4. Compassion needs motivation

Even when adolescents care and have the emotional skills to stay engaged, one additional factor matters: motivation.

In our study, intrinsic prosocial motivation was one of the strongest predictors of helping. Simply put, adolescents who genuinely wanted to help others were more likely to translate concern into action.

This may sound self-evident, but it carries important implications.

Adults often try to encourage helping through external incentives, praise, rewards, or behavioral expectations. While these approaches can influence behavior, our findings suggest that compassionate action is especially powerful when it emerges from internal values and genuine concern for others.

Young people are constantly asking themselves what kind of person they want to be. When helping becomes connected to identity, meaning, and purpose, compassionate action appears more likely to follow.

This suggests that fostering compassion is about more than encouraging kind behavior. It is also about helping young people develop a sense of responsibility toward others and a meaningful connection to shared humanity.

## What gets in the way of compassion?

Taken together, these findings challenge a common assumption.

There is a tendency to treat moments of inaction as moments of moral failure. We see a young person remain silent, fail to intervene, or walk past another person’s suffering, and we assume we understand what happened.

Yet our research suggests that these moments are often more complicated than they appear.

They unfold within social worlds shaped by belonging, friendship, identity, uncertainty, vulnerability, and the deeply human desire to remain connected to others. They are influenced by relationships, social risks, emotional capacities, and personal motivations.

What looks like indifference from a distance may sometimes reflect a struggle between compassion and the realities that make compassionate action difficult.

This perspective shifts the conversation from a question of character to a question of conditions.

Rather than asking whether adolescents are compassionate, we might ask: What conditions help compassion become action?

## Helping caring become action

The encouraging message from this research is that the factors influencing compassionate action are not fixed traits.

Relationships can be strengthened.

School climates can be improved.

Emotional regulation skills can be taught.

Prosocial values can be nurtured.

When we think about compassion this way, the goal becomes larger than helping young people recognize suffering. The goal is helping them develop the capacities that allow caring to become action.

Perhaps this is what adolescence reveals so clearly. The distance between caring and acting is rarely empty space. It is filled with questions about belonging, uncertainty, responsibility, and risk.

Young people are learning to navigate that space every day.

Our responsibility as the adults who support them is not simply to teach them to care. It is to create the relationships, communities, and opportunities that help them act on the care they already possess.

items.articleBody:
*The following article was written as a companion piece for Lewis Richmond’s upcoming* Tricycle *class, “A Buddhist Response to AI: Studying Samsara, Practicing Kindness.”* [Sign up today](https://tricycle.org/events/ai-buddhism-email-program/#signup) *.*

The Dalai Lama has often said that Buddhist practitioners should study samsara. Samsara means the everyday world of ignorance and delusion. His advice is foundational and practical; he is encouraging us to know the sea in which we swim. And because today’s technology is so inescapable and powerful, there is probably no greater magnifier of samsara today than technology, which now includes artificial intelligence. So, like it or not, we Buddhists need to deal with AI; at least we need to study it. As a lifelong Buddhist practitioner and teacher, as well as a former computer professional, I have my doubts as to whether AI is truly intelligent, but, regardless, its influence and power are sweeping the world, and, try as we might, none of us can avoid it. I am proposing that the practices and teachings of Buddhism can be a counterpoint to some of AI’s seductions and a protective shield from some of its dangers. But how, as Buddhists, can we accomplish that? What can we do?

Today, there is a near-war going on between two opposing camps: the realm of living things, and the realm of digital technology. The outcome of this conflict is likely to define every aspect of our long-term future—even whether we survive as a species at all. At least that’s what Nobel prize winner Dr. Geoffrey Hinton—known as the “father of AI”—has warned; other tech gurus have echoed his words. This is serious business. I have given names to these two camps: I call the world of technology “Byteworld,” and the world of living things “Lifeworld.” Byteworld and Lifeworld—these two are arm in arm, marching headlong into unknown territory. Of course Lifeworld (that is, ourselves) created all of Byteworld (as well as Buddhism), but Byteworld is breaking free of its human bonds and going its own way, like some golem-like clay doll magically come to life.

Computer technology arguably began with the invention of the mainframe computer in the 1950s, followed by the personal computer, the internet, smartphones, social media, and, finally, “artificial intelligence.” The biosphere, in contrast, has existed for untold millennia, evolving from single-celled organisms to dinosaurs, parrots, dolphins, elephants, the great apes, and us. Our human achievements are legion: fire, the wheel, great epics and dramas, symphonies and songs, towering cities and civilizations, sailing ships and rockets, myriad forms of civilization and social organization, religion and spiritual life, and, of course, Byteworld itself. Of these I think Lifeworld’s greatest accomplishment is religion and spiritual life—paths leading to inner transformation and an awakened state of compassionate awareness. Buddhism, which has been my life’s study, is such a path.

I know technology from the inside; beginning in 1994, for twenty-five years, I owned and managed a software company whose product was a business-to-business software application that I wrote myself. But before that I spent thousands of hours in meditation on my black cushion, as well as studying Buddhism with some of the best living teachers. So I’ve had a foot in both worlds. I know the thrill that comes from writing a block of computer code and watching it perform its magic in the real world. I also know how urgently our world needs the spiritual healing and compassionate perspective that paths such as Buddhism can provide.

Though I understand how Byteworld works, my refuge has always been the biological wisdom of Lifeworld. When I was younger, it was my hope that this coming age would be one of spiritual awakening, but, instead, I see all the attention, power, and money racing in the other direction: toward the godlike power of technology, a glittering secular deity whose silicon chips and farmland-destroying data centers are replicating like a metallic cancer. How can we rein in this explosive machine?

Technology and AI do have limits. I doubt that AI is on its way to being all-powerful, in spite of what some tech gurus say. These machines of our making emulate only some portion of what our brains can do—mostly their verbal and mathematical skills. There is so much more to the human psyche. Psychologist Howard Gardner has proposed a theory of eight forms of human intelligence. In addition to words and mathematics, he adds music (Mozart), spatial awareness (architects), physical ability (athletes and surgeons), naturalistic knowledge (gardeners), interpersonal intelligence (therapists, ministers, and mediators), and *intra* personal intelligence (the awareness of our inner states and processes). AI excels in words and numbers. But it lacks feeling and true emotion—the relational skills of which Gardner speaks—and an intimacy with the natural world of plants and animals. It’s worth mentioning that “intrapersonal intelligence” is also the domain of meditation, which involves paying attention to our inner physical and mental states. Intrapersonal intelligence, on which Buddhism is built, may be in time a hidden resource that could counterbalance the empires of Byteworld. If so, each of us as Buddhists may have a role to play.

AI offers power, wealth, and control to those few who create and deploy it, but its capacities are narrow compared to the biological wisdom that incorporates emotion, intuition, faith, and religion, the five physical senses, and our 64 trillion cells, each with its own DNA-powered intelligence that we share with the whole biosphere. AI is a kind of miracle, to be sure. There is no question that Byteworld has game, but Lifeworld has so much more. What AI entity could ever experience the grandeur of Beethoven’s musical heart? And, for that matter, what robot could pray?

I suspect that our fascination with the glories of AI will sour in time as its darker capabilities, including weaponization and environmental pollution, come to the fore. To summarize the core message of the Buddha’s path: Each of us is a living Buddha at heart, only waiting to emerge like a butterfly from a cocoon. We don’t need any additional machines or vast data centers in farmland or in space to achieve that. We already have what we need. We are the heirs of the whole biosphere’s intelligent rainforest. Awakening is a birthright for every one of us. Lifeworld offers us untold gifts, including the dharma. That said, the human realm is not an unalloyed good, and technology is not an unalloyed bad. Each domain is complex; each has its gifts as well as dangers.

## Gifts and Dangers of Lifeworld

*Living relationships.* Everything in the world of the living is intrinsically related, but not by bits and bytes. We share with every living thing the pulse of aliveness; we share their DNA, their evolution and adaptability. In a more profound sense we share a living connection with all of reality. Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh calls this connectivity “interbeing,” and it is described in detail in Buddhist scriptures such as the *Avatamsaka Sutra*. Human community and family, the kind we can touch and feel in the presence of others, is foundational; in some ways it is our deepest intelligence. In Buddhism we call that sangha.

*Slowness.* Speed is our new god these days, but the pace of living things is of a different order. Lifeworld is optimized for survival and evolution. Lifeworld is actually neither slow nor fast; it simply marks the pace of being alive. A human baby takes nine months to gestate. It can’t be speeded up. A majestic redwood tree takes a hundred years to grow, or a thousand. It will never be digitized. The vibrancy of all living things, the unfolding of a whole human life from beginning to end, the blossoming of love and of family, each require their appropriate season and timing. Speed will not improve them. Deepfake emulation will not replace them. Life evolves and replicates in slow time.

*Kindness.* The world of the living tends toward kindness; kindness is an artifact of interbeing. Human beings can be cruel, too, but kindness is our higher goal. Digital intelligence can emulate kindness; already chatbots have been trained to tell us how good we look and how great our ideas are. But true kindness occurs through aliveness. It arises from the interpersonal intelligence that Howard Gardner describes, and it is intrinsic to sangha. The kindness we have can never be replaced by a machine. What is most true about kindness is that we need more of it.

*Dangers of the human realm.* Long ago the Buddha identified the dark side of the human psyche with his teaching of the “three unwholesome roots”—greed, aversion, and egoistic delusion. These “three poisons” have sullied and darkened every human generation, including ours. Just because we are Buddhas in the making doesn’t mean that we are blameless. Innately we are good, but that quality is too often clouded.

## Dangers and Gifts of Byteworld

AI is not just chatbots. AI is rapidly being integrated in every aspect of human life. In business, AI is taking over marketing, customer service, and hiring; it is also now doing much entry-level computer programming. In banking, AI does fraud protection, lending, and customer service. Its military uses are rapidly increasing too. Candidly, AI is everywhere. These new AI roles present many dangers; here are just a few of them.

*Addiction.* Social media is already addictive, and harms children; AI is making it more so. Criminals using AI have discovered new ways to defraud, to steal, to harass, to invade privacy, to destroy reputations, even to kill. Terrorists may soon use AI to create a weaponized virus with no cure. Has all this AI-enhanced digital connectivity been worth it, just so we can ask our chatbot for the best recipe for banana bread?

*Jobs.* The fear that AI and humanoid robots driven by AI will replace jobs is everywhere. People say they are afraid for their livelihoods and their very future due to AI. The deeper issue is that for the most part the creators of AI and the politicians who make the rules don’t seem to care that much about people’s worries. Are we on the cusp of major social discontent, even disorder in the streets? AI riots?

*Environmental Impact.* In order to do its work, Byteworld requires huge data centers, many the size of fifteen football fields. They are sprouting up everywhere: in previously quiet suburbs; on farmland that once grew crops for food; on the edge of big cities where there is power and water to satisfy their cooling needs. There are already thousands of these centers supporting the digital “cloud”; it is estimated that in the next ten years, to support AI, 3,000 more of these monster construction projects will be built just in the US, with many more in other countries. Each of them requires vast amounts of water and electricity; many also have huge diesel- or gas-powered turbines that pollute the air. These centers are also noisy; those who live near them say that their sound is a loud sleep-disturbing hum. Some local governments are fighting back, but there are billions of dollars to be made by building out this AI infrastructure. When there is that kind of money to be made, ethics and care tend to go out the window.

*Technology’s Gifts.* To be fair, AI has also brought many new benefits. In the realm of medicine alone, AI is already contributing lifesaving technologies such as early cancer detection. It is speeding all manner of research and helps with weather prediction, eldercare, education, and so much more. These benefits are bound to expand with each passing year.

## My Religion Is Kindness

The Dalai Lama has often said, “My religion is kindness.” Because this is such a simple statement, people may not realize how profound it is. He doesn’t only mean “Kindness is valuable and good.” He means that Buddhism as a wisdom practice transforms us into people who are unconditionally kind. The Buddhist term for that type of person is bodhisattva. Lifeworld is the crucible where this kind of compassion can be nurtured.

Once, when the Dalai Lama was asked if he was angry at the Chinese, he replied, “The Chinese have taken so much from us. I won’t let them take my state of mind.” Even in the face of that pain, he maintained his kind heart. I was, for a time, the personal attendant of renowned Vietnamese Buddhist monk Thich Nhat Hanh. He spoke softly and carefully, as though each word were a treasure. The sound of his voice itself, and the way he lifted the cup of tea I had poured for him, radiated kindness.

For my own teacher, Shunryu Suzuki Roshi, kindness was second nature. I witnessed, so many times, when he reached out to help someone or touch a person who needed his care. One time, I came to meditation early in the morning, and there, on the front steps, was Suzuki, quietly talking to a homeless man. As I stepped past them to enter the building, he didn’t look up. He was doing his work.

This unconditional kindness is, I think, the most precious thing in the world. I fear that the implacable march of technology will crush this treasure. I fear that Byteworld will toss it aside as unnecessary, seeing it as a weakness, dismissing it as unable to make money or wield power—an obsolete quality that human beings will no longer need.

I don’t want that to happen. I want kindness to survive, and not just to survive but to prosper. I want everyone to see through the false promise of a light speed digital future and remember what binds us together and connects us to all life—kindness. Without kindness, I fear, we will become wan and hollow. As the Dalai Lama has said, our religion as Buddhists is kindness. Kindness is the best of who we are. It is our not so invisible power.

## Breathwalking with Byteworld

In the course of pondering Lifeworld and Byteworld, I have created a library of contemplative exercises to help us experience the difference between them. Here is one called “Breathwalking with Byteworld.” It uses a smartphone to illustrate how Byteworld takes us away from ourselves, and how we can return to ourselves by walking in awareness—a venerable Buddhist practice.

To begin, stand in a quiet uncrowded place—a hallway in your house or an unpopulated outdoor path—and lift up your smartphone. Open the phone’s camera app so that you can see the scene in front of you. To start, let the phone drop to your side and begin walking slowly, feet a shoulder-width apart, one step for each exhale, so that your whole body flows with movement and your mind observes it with attention and awareness. In ancient days, Buddhist monks would spend hours each day walking just like this on their verandas or in forests.

Now, lift up your phone and look at it. Watch the scene in your camera unfold while you continue to walk. Notice how the pixel version of what you are seeing gradually absorbs all your attention, while the awareness of your body slowly recedes. The scene you see is almost the same as without your phone, but it is an emulation, a deepfake, if you will. Everywhere, these days, we see people absorbed in that phone world—in airport lobbies, restaurants, classrooms, on sidewalks, even in a moving car—people glued to their phone, watching the alternate universe it presents. Have we all become phone zombies, walking around holding up these shiny rectangles in front of our faces? Sometimes it seems that way.

Now, shift gears again, let the hand that holds your phone drop down, and return to the awareness of breath and your body as you continue to walk. Feel the transition, the bump in the road as the familiar physical world returns and the emulated imagery of the phone screen goes away. The phone is more than a passive copycat. We know now that the apps, texts, photos, and videos on that phone can cause harm. They can hurt children. In the moving car of a distracted texting driver, they can kill. By practicing Breathwalking with Byteworld you can bring the awareness exercise of Buddhist practice to the fore and disempower this deceptive device.

More and more people are becoming aware of how technology is distorting their reality. There are now paid phone apps that lock your phone out for a time, forcing you to give it up when you lack the willpower to do it yourself. You can also go on vacation to an expensive resort that offers a phone-free environment; you give them your phone when you register. These remedies are salves and medicines; look for there to be more of them in the future.

## Looking Ahead

It is hard to say what will happen with all this mad swirl of technological change. There are as many predictions as there are savants to utter them. The truth is no one knows. Meantime, to return to the question that began this essay, *what should we as Buddhists do?*

One possibility is to escape, to remove ourselves as much as possible from the influence of technology and AI. Buddhism’s monastic tradition seems to offer that option. Monastic life is one form of “living off the grid,” staying far from the buzz of the big city, in hidden valleys where everyone knows your name, where people have put away their phones, unplugged their devices from the internet while they tend their own vegetable gardens and write notes to each other in longhand simply because it is more beautiful.

But there is another option besides escape. To paraphrase Pope Leo, “We shouldn’t reject technology but prevent it from dominating humanity.” Buddhists can have a role in that. Bodhisattvas may train in the monastery, but they don’t stay there forever. The vow of the bodhisattva says, “However many beings there are in the world, I vow to liberate them, to care for them all, be kind to them all.” This vow is a commitment not to escape but to engage. As Buddhists we can study the samaras of technology to become more skillful at helping, even as we continue the transformative practices of studying ourselves. We can choose to live in the light of kind action. When there is an opportunity to help, we do not hesitate; when an opportunity doesn’t immediately present itself, we practice patience, tend to our practice and wait. That opportunity will come soon enough.

We can, each in our own way, become exemplars of a life that upholds the highest human values and the deepest inter- and intrapersonal human intelligence, even as AI and its manic golems sweep the world. The bodhisattva vow manifests an awareness and an intelligence that no machine or digital brain can match. We Buddhists dedicate our lives to it, and uphold it as long as we can until others rise to take our place. Even in the face of the loudest criers of technological doom—who may, in the end, be wrong—we keep confidence in that vow.

May it be so.
